subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, again we are discussing this bill which has been around here since December. Obviously, the reason we are still discussing it is the recent failure of the various governments involved, both provincial and federal, to reach some sort of agreement or consensus between the oil producers and consumers and the federal government as to what the price of oil should be, so that it
29557-30^2

April 15, 1975
Oil and Petroleum
can be of benefit to the industry and to the oil producing provinces and so that the industry may continue to expand and to supply the needs of our country. In reaching a decision as to what should be a reasonable price for oil, account should also be taken of the fact that Canadian consumers should be sheltered from some of the worst effects of the world petroleum situation. We should rejoice in our good fortune that our consumers are not exposed to the full world price and do not have to make the adjustments that would be necessary if the world price were adopted in this country.
The recent federal-provincial conference ended without a national price being set and with disagreement between the producing provinces, the consuming provinces and the federal government. One might consider federal-provincial conferences as a means of solving problems which exist between the federal authority-which presumably functions for the over-all good of Canadians in all regions, and for the good of the provinces which put forward views reflecting their regional situations-and the provinces. This method of producing binding and often far reaching legislation which will affect the country as a whole is assuming greater importance because governments are becoming increasingly involved in various programs in light of the various economic situations which necessitate government action.
In this case there was an outward attempt by the governments to set the price of oil at the wellhead. Federal-provincial conferences will certainly become more and more frequent and more and more involved in economic matters such as price fixing if we keep on moving away from a market economy to a rigid form of government controlled and government directed economy. It is doubtful whether this type of conference is the best forum in which to settle problems such as this, and certainly it seems to make the role of the elected representative irrelevant, whether he be a member of the provincial or federal legislature or whether he be a member of the government or of the opposition. As I said, the recent federal-provincial conference was not successful. Perhaps it was doomed to failure because of the failure of the governments concerned to reach a preliminary agreement in the matter of setting a reasonable oil price before the conference was held.
It seems to me that a number of issues are involved in the bill before us. They affect regional interests, regional needs and regional welfare. In considering this bill, all too often regional interests override the national interest. We must consider-I believe this has been overlooked in our debate until now-what will be the international effect of our action in setting the price for oil in Canada.
This bill is breaking new ground in that the federal government is intruding into provincial jurisdiction by setting the price of a natural resource at a time when it is doubtful that a national emergency exists. By and large, there have been many cases, except in wartime, when the federal government has felt constrained to override provincial jurisdictions and to set prices on a national level. For instance, just recently in the matter of the two-price system for wheat, the Government of Canada set the price of wheat for Canadian consumption at approximately $4.75 a bushel when the world price had been for some

months previously nearly $6 a bushel, as a result of which wheat producers were selling at a loss of approximately $1 a bushel. I do not think anyone could construe the situation at that time as being a national emergency. The federal government's decision in that case was supported by enabling legislation whereby provinces delegated power to the Wheat Board to assume control over wheat production.
I doubt whether the present situation with regard to oil can be considered to be a national emergency as defined in section 92(10)(c) of the British North America Act. In my opinion, such an emergency would only arise in the event of hostilities involving this country in a war, or having the effect of cutting off offshore imports such as if there were an outbreak of hostilities in the Middle East. No such emergency has arisen as yet. Indeed, we have a reasonable supply of oil to meet our own needs, at a price greatly below the world level. What we are discussing is how much our price should rise, if at all, and in what manner will the moneys accruing from this price increase serve to secure our supplies for the future. We are certainly not involved in any emergency situation at present.
This bill is of fundamental importance to our nation. Through it, the federal government is attempting to set the price of a resource which is found mainly in one or two provinces. If the government is successful in doing this, it is obvious that provincial jurisdictions will be reduced to asking for hand-outs from the federal government. Another point to be considered is that if the price of oil can be set unilaterally by the federal government, then obviously the price of other resources such as copper, nickel and coal could similarly be set by the government. Furthermore, a good case could be made for setting the price of newsprint, lumber and agricultural products in this country.
This bill assumes even greater importance when we realize that at a time when there is no real emergency, the federal government is attempting to set the price of a resource at whatever level it considers appropriate. Mr. Chairman, this legislation represents a far reaching intrusion into provincial jurisdiction and an extension into the market economy of this country. Before it is used to set a price, real bargaining and real consultation should take place between the federal government, representing the interests of the country as a whole-but, in effect, largely central Canada-and the producing provinces which are mainly Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia.
I think we are agreed that we should not insulate ourselves from the world economy unless it is very disadvantageous. In the finance committee today, the Minister of Finance, in answering a question, suggested that two-price systems for products held open a very real possibility that they would be looked upon as trade barriers similar to tariffs and that retaliatory action would be taken.
Certainly, if an American company or any other foreign company were meeting competition from a Canadian company in its own market, and if the advantage to the Canadian company were dependent on a reduced price for oil or gas used in the manufacture of that product, then the foreign company would be quite justified in urging its
April 15, 1975

government to erect a tariff barrier against the Canadian product. We ourselves witness the example of our textile industry always complaining bitterly about the low wage structure of Far Eastern countries undermining the industry, and seeking appropriate protection. Similar charges could be levelled at our exports which were dependent on low level oil and gas prices. Obviously, the price of oil and gas should rise to world levels, but we in Canada can be fortunate enough to take some time to reach this level. If the price is to be set below the world level, it must certainly be high enough and the industry must receive enough of it so that exploration will be carried on and security of supply will be furthered as much as possible.
But what has happened to the situation in Canada? There was an increase in the price of oil to $6.50 a barrel. But has this increased exploration activity? Of course not. The November budget of the Minister of Finance scuppered this possibility. There is no point in raising the price of oil unless exploration and development is carried on. Surely the main culprit is the federal government. In his budget, the Minister of Finance, in attempting to prevent the provinces from having accrue to them the benefits the increase in the world price of oil and gas would have brought them, has put in place a punitive federal tax. I think it has to be realized that until recently we have really had to pay money to have people explore for oil and gas. It has been suggested by the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain that there is only one time for one jurisdiction to steal, but I think we have to recognize that the provinces were there first. The BNA Act gave the right to have this revenue accrue to the provincial jurisdictions, and if the federal government is going to become involved it certainly should be done by negotiation.
There are some figures in a bar graph of where the oil dollar goes. It shows that at $3.80 a barrel the oil industry received 50 cents for lifting, $1.35 for exploration and drilling costs, and 53 cents for industry retention, with the provincial government receiving $1.15 and the federal government 27 cents. After the increase in April to $6.50, the industry's share went to $1.17, whereas the provincial government received $2.97 and the federal government 51 cents. After the November 18 budget the industry retention figure went down to 13 cents. This is the situation in Alberta. The provincial government received $3.34 and the federal government $1.18. In other words, the increase in the federal tax has had the effect of leaving the industry with considerably less than it received when the price was $3.80.
At the recent energy conference Mr. Blakeney, the Premier of Saskatchewan, said that if we just have a flat rate of increase, the big winner will be the federal government; it will receive the lion's share. In other words, without changes this act in itself will not in any way get at the real problem, which is to allow the industry to function better and to produce more supplies and more reserves of gas and oil by the two governments, leaving more money in the industry.
The real problem with this bill and the whole oil pricing system, if we are to have the price set well below the world price, is the failure of the provincial and federal governments to reach common ground. Surely, under the BNA Act and by all historic patterns of tradition, the
Oil and Petroleum
provincial governments were first in the field of taxation of resources, and if in the national interest of the federal government must take more revenue from resource industries, it should not be done high-handedly and unilaterally. The problem affecting resource industries is not just confined to a vendetta with Alberta; it affects every province in Canada because almost all the provinces have sizeable resource industries.
I spoke to a respected member of the other place, who has been here a long time and is well aware of the structure under which our government operates, about the fact that the provinces were vested under the BNA Act with ownership of resources. He aptly said that while ownership remained with the provinces, federal taxing power over the last 20 or 25 years had effectively reduced the control of the resource industries by the provinces and subverted it largely to the federal field. In effect, the federal government, through the taxation system, has been muscling in on the provincial field.
I think many of our problems as a nation are getting worse and reaching more and more Canadians, especially western Canadians who are becoming extremely skeptical about the advantages of confederation. The federal government is attempting to take over taxation in the resource field and in other fields. At the same time, it has been attempting to slough off many of the shared-cost programs which are so expensive and to divest itself of the responsibility in this field by giving a few taxation points to the provinces. The actions of the federal government in the field of resource taxation have been disastrous for industry and for the country. In today's Globe and Mail there is a suggestion that the Ontario mining industry is in a bad way. Mr. O'Brien, quoted in the Globe and Mail, states:
"There is a danger" ... "that Canadian mining companies, which are among the most productive and efficient in the world, are clearly being discouraged from maintaining that position."
So it is not just the oil industry levelling this charge at the federal government; it is the suggestion of many Albertans that the oil industry has been sold out by the federal government. This bill does not in any way solve the fundamental problem that confronts us, which is, how much of the oil dollar should go to the government, and how much to the oil industry? One cannot help agreeing to a considerable extent with the Premier of Ontario who asked, what is the point of increasing the cost of oil and gas unless enough of it goes to the oil industry to make it productive and increase exploration?
Yesterday, the Minister of Finance agreed in the finance committee that the reduction of oil exports to the United States would greatly increase our difficulties in balance of payments problems with that country. Many Canadians have clamoured loud and long for the cessation of exports of oil and gas to the United States. This year alone this would cost us perhaps a billion dollars in lost export trade. Are these same Canadians now prepared to face the consequences of this enormous loss in export trade?
The Minister of Finance has said we expect capital inflows to cover this balance of payments deficit, but if capital comes into the country it further increases foreign

April 15, 1975
Oil and Petroleum
ownership of our mines, factories and resources. For instance, in the finance committee a report was given that a certain type of Saskatchewan crude is being forced out of the United States market because of the export tax. Apparently this type of crude at the present time can only be refined in Minneapolis. There is no use for the crude in Canada, yet the export tax has diminished its use in the United States. This is a clear example of what will happen when we apply government rules indiscriminately.
Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that this bill will solve the problem of how to set the price for oil and gas. The government has given no indication of what it regards as a reasonable increase, if any, in the price. We should have a better definition of what is a true price for oil in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I will not detain the committee long, although I have other comments to make on a future occasion during the debate. I want to deal with some misstatements by the minister yesterday while they are fresh in my mind and in the minds of hon. members. I am not reluctant to do this because I feel under a certain obligation, following the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver South, to try to supplement the lectures on law which the minister must have received in college and to help him in his knowledge of the law. It is always a pleasure to help promising young lawyers, and I feel an obligation to do so now.
I understand some of the minister's problems,, because he has said his advice was received from the Minister of Justice. No wonder he has misconceived the law. When I was a young, freshly-minded barrister and went to the Peace River country to practice, there was there a fine old judge whose knowledge of the law was not very good, nor was his comprehension of the facts. At every assizes, however, he made sure that a lawyer won at least one case. He was known throughout the profession as "Old Judge Necessity". Your Honour will understand that, knowing the motto "Necessity knows no law". I suggest that when the minister gets his legal opinions from the Minister of Justice, this motto should be applied.
I know that the minister has a responsibility to take advice from the Minister of Justice, as the first law officer of the Crown, and his officials. But that does not mean his opinion is always right. The law books of this country are replete with cases where the federal government and the provincial governments, acting on the advice of counsel attached to their departments of justice or solicitors general, have legislated accordingly and have seen the legislation struck down. Because the Minister of Justice and his officials have given this minister some advice does not mean that that advice is necessarily correct. Speaking directly to the point, Mr. Chairman, yesterday the minister referred to the CalOil case as being an indication of the position he had taken, when he said as reported at page 4775 of Hansard:
I really need not do so-
He was referring to the case I had raised.
-in view of the fact that the Supreme Court of Canada has decided, in relation to the jurisdiction of the National Energy Board, that the Government of Canada does have jurisdiction to set the price of oil and oil products-

That was the CalOil case. There may be a recent citation, and if I am wrong I hope the minister will correct me and I will accept it. As I understand the situation, however, the Supreme Court of Canada did not sit on that case and did not hear the appeal. I have searched for the citation, unsuccessfully. Perhaps the minister will give it to me.

I appreciate getting that information from the minister, because I was not able to find it. Apart from that fact which was only collateral, my understanding of the situation is that in that case there was a problem with regard to the jurisdiction of the National Energy Board because the so-called Ottawa Valley line had been drawn in such a way as to sever the province of Ontario into two parts. The decision of a former deputy minister of justice, now Mr. Justice Jackett of the Federal Court who wrote the judgment in the first CalOil case, was to the effect that it was not within the jurisdiction of the federal government, or the National Energy Board as its agent, to enact regulations which would in any way interfere with the movement of oil and petroleum products from one part of the province to another.
Immediately after that, as I understand the citation, the National Energy Board met and amended the regulation. Then in a subsequent case in which the same parties were involved, Mr. Justice Dumoulin gave effect to the views of the National Energy Board and the federal government and declared that in fact the changed regulations did permit this prohibition to continue. That was, I think, somewhat different from the situation cited by the minister yesterday which dealt with the question of price. The case, as I read it, in its initial stages-unless some other extraneous issue was raised in the argument before the Supreme Court-was not concerned with price but with movement. I think that disposes of the authority which the minister has cited.
The other point I want to deal with now is the statement made by the minister yesterday. He suggested that the Diefenbaker government passed the National Energy Board Act in 1959 for the purpose of controlling and fixing prices, and that the act gave, and was intended to give, to the federal government the right which the present government is now claiming. I challenge that position. I was here as a member and recall the debate which took place at that time. I have researched some of the debates of 1959 and subsequent years. Allow me to read a statement made by Hon. Gordon Churchill, a distinguished member of the Diefenbaker government. He was minister of trade and commerce and was responsible for piloting the legislation
April 15, 1975

through the House. He said, as recorded on page 3927 of Hansard for May 22, 1959:
Gas prices at the point of production are regarded by the provinces of origin as being under their jurisdiction, and gas prices to the ultimate consumer are controlled by the province in which consumption takes place. The government of Canada has had the power to exercise control over the price of gas being exported under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act-
About that position there is no argument. The minister who was then piloting the bill through the House indicated in the first statement that, beyond any shadow of doubt, gas prices at the point of production were regarded by the provinces of origin as being under their jurisdiction. Mr. Churchill went on to say, as recorded on page 3928:
It is not the practice-
I interpolate by saying that it is neither the practice nor the law.
-in peacetime to control prices or commodities in internal trade, but it is normal to control transportation or transmission charges, as in the case of railway freight rates.
That statement related to the purpose of the enactment of the National Energy Board Act and the establishment of the board. The federal government, through the use of controls and conditions attached to interprovincial trade and through provisions governing the transportation of oil and gas contained in that bill, was enabled to exert some influence on the price of goods at the point of destination. Finally, Mr. Churchill said, as recorded on page 3931 of Hansard:
Also I would emphasize again that we have sought with great care to avoid any interference with the proper jurisdiction of the provinces.
I must say that the last statement does not apply to the present government. Let me now deal with what the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands said. I was surprised at his position. Let me refer the hon. member to what Mr. Bert Herridge, a member of his party, said on May 18, 1959, as recorded on page 3777 of Hansard:
It is true that intraprovineial fuel and power matters are exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provinces. That is as it should be... and we in this group would not want to change that one iota.
I shall refer to quotations from other sources later in this debate. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the statements I have read, and others, make it clear that the government of the day in 1959, in introducing this legislation did not intend to violate ruthlessly the constitution by fixing prices at the wellhead, as the government seeks to do in the present instance. That, I think, was a position of common sense.
The position which my leader took last night is the position my party has always taken. We say that you should attempt to secure consensus on a multilateral basis among all involved parties. If that is not possible, you must consider the possibility of securing an agreement between a producing province and the federal government acting, as it must, on behalf of the people of Canada. But if that agreement is not possible, if for any reason it cannot be reached, that by itself does not automatically give the federal government jurisdiction. Surely it must first await the arrival of an emergency situation before invoking the
Oil and Petroleum
peace, order and good government clause of the constitution and thereby securing that jurisdiction.
It may well be that present conditions in the world, present conditions in Canada which are distinct from conditions in 1959, the extent to which energy and energy use has become a supremely important element in the social and economic world in which we live, present shortages of energy and apprehended shortages which may be realized in one or two years, may necessitate such changes in our consideration of the constitution as will permit the federal government to invoke that clause. All the same, we are far removed from the situation which applied in 1919 and 1920 when, in the Fort Frances case, the privy council laid down rules with regard to the right of the federal government to intervene in property and civil rights matters which come solely within the jurisdiction of the provincial government.
I readily concede that, considering the situation existing in the world today-we are awaiting reports from boards about potential energy reserves in this country-and considering that our whole social and economic structure is predicated on the use of energy, it is now far easier for the federal government to make that kind of declaration; it is easier than it would have been in 1920 or 1921, or even in 1959. For those reasons we have adopted our position. That position is consistent with the position we took in 1959 as a party, and consistent with our responsibilities as an opposition.
We say that if an emergency does not exist, the federal government does not have the power it suggests it has. We , work under a finely-tuned federal system in which the producing province has the right to fix the wellhead price and to dispose of the product at the wellhead to people within the province. Clearly, the consuming province has every right by law to fix the price of the product within that province. In addition, the federal government, through its exercise of powers governing the regulation of trade and commerce and the transportation of a commodity through a pipeline, or commodities involved in interprovincial trade, may affect substantially the price of the commodity as it flows from the producing to the consuming province. But in a federal system, if there is no emergency it must, of necessity, bring all three parties-hopefully there will be three, but in any event there will be two-together and, in exercising leadership, work out an agreement.
Before I sit down, let me make a statement which we shall make over and over again. Unless that emergency exists, failure to reach agreement does not vest the government with powers it does not have.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has referred to the CalOil case. May I refer to the case decided in 1971, on appeal, by the full Supreme Court. Mr. Justice Pigeon gave the opinion of the court. The case dealt with a statement of principle. The hon. gentleman spoke about the wellhead price. In the case before the court, the question of the consumer price in the province of Ontario was at stake. The principle of federal regulation was attacked. One of the parties purporting to sell in the Ontario market argued that the restrictions imposed in the National Energy Board Act were beyond the powers of the federal government in so far as they dealt with the regula-

April 15, 1975
Oil and Petroleum
tion of trade and commerce. I quote from Mr. Justice Pigeon what seems to be the clearest enunciation of the principle, to be found at page 477 of Dominion Law Reports, volume 20, third series:
As noted by Dumoulin, J., Lord Tomlin's fourth proposition in the Fish Canneries case... is:
(4) There can be a domain in which provincial and Dominion legislation may overlap, in which case neither legislation will be ultra vires if the field is clear, but if the field is not clear and the two legislations meet the Dominion legislation must prevail...
This principle was recently applied by this court in such cases as-
He then cites a number of authorities. This is the statement of principle:
It is clear, therefore, that the existence and extent of provincial regulatory authority over specific trades within the province is not the sole criterion to be considered in deciding whether a federal regulation affecting such a trade is invalid. On the contrary, it is no objection when the impugned enactment is an integral part of a scheme for the regulation of international or interprovincial trade, a purpose that is clearly outside provincial jurisdiction and within the exclusive federal field of action.
In other words, the power under the constitution has been given to the federal government in certain cases to regulate trade, including the setting of prices in a particular trade, where that trade is part of an interprovincial or international system of regulation. That is precisely what is provided in this case. Hon. members will have noted the bill is very careful to make it clear that it is to apply to transactions related to the removal of products from a province, removal across a provincial boundary to other , parts of Canada or for export.
One of the wisest things the hon. gentleman said yesterday is that perhaps it is not a useful exercise to debate points of law in this parliament. I accept the basis of that.
I merely put the proposition of the Supreme Court of Canada on the record and let hon. members and readers of Hansard judge for themselves.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a question? Is it not a fact that that case involved a situation where CalOil was importing oil into Canada, and the National Energy Board-as it was entitled to, being the appropriate federal authority-set conditions, with regard to the importation of that oil, as to the place to which the oil was to be brought and utilized. This was because originally an attempt was made to take it from one part of one province into another. The decision of Mr. Justice Jackett was against the federal government.
The federal government made no attempt to appeal that decision. It was quite prepared to accept that decision which said, in effect, that the federal government, exercising its right, could not make regulations prohibiting or in any way interfering with the movement of oil from one part of a province to another part: it was prohibited and the federal government was out of court when it attempted to do that. That decision was not appealed. The case had nothing to do with price; it involved the import of oil into Canada with conditions attached.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have enjoyed listening to this erudite discussion between the hon. member for Peace River and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on the constitutionality of the veto clauses of Bill C-32 and whether in fact the government has the authority to set prices. I cannot claim legal training other than that which I have gained from sitting in this House for some 2lA years.
It seems obvious, from sheer logic and by just examining the facts as presented, that the veto clauses are contrary to the constitution, the British North America Act, and the Mineral Transfers Act of 1930 which transferred to the western provinces jurisdiction and ownership of all natural resources. More fundamentally on the legal question, the Mineral Transfers Act, as an amendment to the BNA Act, states in plain English that the resources belong to the provinces: they are owned by the provinces. I submit that if one says "Fine," there is no contest in that regard. However, if the price, the markets, indirectly the royalties, and the transportation shall be dictated by the federal government, what rights of ownership are there? Ownership becomes totally meaningless because in fact total control rests in the hands of the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
In view of the very simple reasoning in the Mineral Transfers Act of 1930 that natural resources, including oil and gas and the royalties derived therefrom, are owned by the provincial governments of Canada, these veto clauses which give the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources the authority unilaterally to set the prices of crude oil and natural gas are contrary to the constitution: they are unconstitutional.
This is the third occasion on which we have discussed this question. In the last parliament there was a predecessor bill, Bill C-18, which was never passed by the House. In this parliament we had the introduction of Bill C-32. Bill C-18 was a bad bill, and because of the minority situation the government was unable to impose it upon the House of Commons and the country. Having achieved a majority on July 8, they introduced Bill C-32, which is worse than Bill C-18. Bill C-18 in the previous parliament was bad; Bill C-32 is worse. As a result of gaining a majority, they expect they can now impose this bill on parliament and, therefore, on the country.
During our deliberations before Christmas, many arguments in opposition to this bill were presented by members of our party and members of the New Democratic Party. We indicated that we objected to the bill. Alternatives were presented to the government in terms of the availability of other acts now in existence, such as the Export and Import Permits Act, through which the government could accomplish the purposes of Bill C-32, namely, a uniform price for crude oil across Canada at something less than the world market price and impose an export charge and subsidy program for the consumers of imported oil east of the Ottawa Valley line. I thought, on the basis of those arguments and the fact that these alternatives were made known to the government, that
April 15, 1975

they had decided to withdraw the bill. Indeed, they did withdraw it and supplementary estimates were introduced to look after the subsidy program.
Unfortunately, however, it appears I was naive, because this week we began again our consideration of Bill C-32, brought back-coincidentally, I am sure-just a few days after the failure of the conference of first ministers to agree on what the price of crude oil in this country should be after July 30. I am sure I would be forgiven for reaching the conclusion that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has made a political judgment and concluded that because of the failure of this conference, we in the opposition who have opposed the bill might now be more ready to give the government the power it seeks. If the minister is acting on that assumption, I am afraid he is mistaken. He is mistaken if he now thinks we will go along by giving parliamentary sanction to the powers requested in the bill before us.

speechtext:
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance has given his financial judgment as to what has caused this disenchantment on the part of the energy industries in Canada. I can only suggest that while the energy minister is in Sudbury, I arrange some meetings for him in Calgary, where he will soon be straightened out on the situation. He is totally wrong. There is no question that return on investment is a significant factor. The oil companies have no confidence that the government will let them remain a viable industry and receive a reasonable return on their investment. They feel that some of the Arab emirates will in fact be more open, honest and fair in their dealings with them than will the Government of Canada.
It is shocking that such a situation should exist, Mr. Chairman. The provision of these veto clauses in Bill C-32 is one of the main reasons for this feeling. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has virtually managed to destroy the industry or to do it great damage without the sort of powers that he will be given by this bill. Imagine what he could do if he had such powers! He would wipe out the industry in a day.
This bill is not going to improve Canada's supply situation. The most serious problem that we as a nation face today-a problem that must be faced but which apparently no one in the government is facing-arises from the predictions made in the National Energy Board report of last December to the effect that this year we will become a net importer of crude oil. Within six years, according to the report, we will be unable to supply from Canadian sources the area west of the Ottawa Valley. Since the Borden line was introduced in 1959 with the national oil policy, the area west of the Ottawa Valley line has been supplied by Canadian crude oil. We produced more than the market could absorb at that time. However, within six years we will be unable to produce enough to satisfy that market, and Toronto will be in the position of having to rely on imported crude oil, which will be subject to all the vagaries of the Middle East political situation and the consequences that will flow therefrom.
With regard to natural gas, within three years there will be insufficient natural gas produced in Canada to supply Canadian markets. There will have to be rationing or the importation of very high-priced natural gas which will have to be shipped to the country in liquid state, thus driving up the price enormously.
This bill will not add one barrel of oil to Canada's proven recoverable reserves, reserves that have been declining steadily since 1971 and which will lead to the shortage I have just been talking about. This should give us greatest cause for concern and we should redress the situation. Adding to the proven recoverable reserves should be the number one priority objective of a national

energy policy and the number one concern of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Any evidence of such concern is far from obvious to this observer or to anybody else. If there is any concern at all, it goes no further than some gnashing of teeth and biting of fingernails. There is nothing in the way of positive initiative to try to turn the situation around. Quite the contrary. What we have are veto clauses in this bill which can only make the situation worse.
The bill will do nothing but exacerbate an already alarming equipment drain from the country. The latest estimates indicate that 95 drilling rigs have left or are leaving Canada since the whole energy confrontation started. This in itself is a symptom of the malaise that exists. It is symptomatic of the fact that exploration and development-the search for crude oil, for the new oil supplies that Canada will need for the future-have stopped or have significantly decreased. The owners of the rigs, Canadian companies all, have found that to seek employment they must either move south or to other areas. It is incredible, but nonetheless the fact is that Canada is the only petrolific area in the entire world that has seen a reduction in exploration and development in the industry in the last year. What a testimonial to the energy policies of this country and to any confidence that this government will look after Canada's future energy needs!
Finally, and perhaps most importantly, the bill will certainly not bring about better federal-provincial relations. Far from it. I find it incredible that a government which originally was elected on the basis that it would bring about national unity, that it would pull the country together, that it deplored the divisions existing in the country and that it would make national unity its number one priority and goal, should turn around and resort to tactics that are themselves driving great wedges into the country.
Many of my hon. friends discount statements such as that. They say they are not true, that the feelings of alienation I am talking about are frustration. They accuse me of indulging in rhetoric as an argument to try to maintain the privileged position that these companies now have. That is not the case, Mr. Chairman. The situation is very serious. Those of us who are devoting our lives to the service of this country want to see the country strong and united in all parts. A continuation of these kinds of tactics and the use of brute force in the form of Bill C-32 can only make things worse, exacerbating an already bad situation.
The time has long since passed that the minister and the government should alter their direction and stop trying to pit one part of the country against another. Let them work things out in the manner traditional in Canada, which is the way we have always worked things out. There are some good, well meaning people in all jurisdictions in Canada. If the tactics adopted were conciliatory rather than confrontation tactics, this would go a long way toward reducing feelings of alienation.
For those reasons and many more, we simply cannot go along with this bill. It is a bad bill. It requires amendment because in its present form it will do great damage to the
April 15, 1975

country. In essence, this bill would give parliamentary sanction to the decision of September 4, 1973, when the government introduced a price freeze on crude oil. That particular decision on that Tuesday after the Labour Day weekend, when the Prime Minister, in response to pressure from the New Democratic Party, made a statement about inflation and the anti-inflationary policies of the government and indicated that there would be a temporary price freeze on crude oil, marked a very clear division between a situation in the country in which the future, certainly in terms of the energy industries and energy supplies, looked rosy and bright to the situation we have today of doom and gloom.
We might compare the situation in the oil and energy industries between the summer of 1973 and the present time. In 1973, the industry, after a fairly long period of limited markets and low cash flows because of low prices, was in a period of tremendous optimism and enthusiasm. All the companies, particularly the Canadian independents which were doing most of the drilling in the great plains area of the western provinces, were geared up to massive programs of resource exploration and development. These companies had expansion programs. There were shortages of personnel such as geophysicists and petroleum engineers, but financing for exploration and resource development was not a particular problem.
As I indicated earlier, basically since 1971 we have been facing a decrease in respect of proven recoverable reserves in Canada. However, there is no doubt in my mind that if the exploration and development efforts planned to take place in 1973 had been carried out, the situation would be reversed and we would be in a position of having increased proven recoverable reserves; we would be in a situation where Canada would be self-sufficient well into the future if anybody cared to extrapolate. The government in July, 1973, introduced an energy policy document called "An Energy Policy for Canada; Phase One," which contained a great deal of very useful information. It contained a very well conducted analysis of Canada's energy situation and some recommendations for a national energy policy that would have made sense and been good for Canada.
Things looked very good in that period: Canada's prospects looked excellent. However, just two short months after this energy policy was introduced, the Prime Minister announced on September 4 a freeze on the price of crude oil. In something less than a month later, because of the provisions under the National Energy Board Act that Canada could not export oil and gas at less than fair market value, it was necessary to invent the export tax. Both moves, the freeze and the export tax, were taken with no consultation with the producing provinces. It was announced by the Prime Minister that this was the way it would be. There was no consultation and, understandably, there was concern on the part of the producing provinces that this move should be taken.
I refer particularly to Saskatchewan and Alberta because in that summer there were three commodities the price of which was controlled-beef, wheat and oil. It would be difficult to name three other commodities more important to the economy of those two provinces. Understandably, the people of Saskatchewan and Alberta asked
Oil and Petroleum
why these three commodities were frozen under the government's anti-inflationary program. They wondered whether political reasons might be involved. I am afraid we know the answer. Prior to the imposition of the price freeze and the export tax, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources indicated that this was just temporary, that the freeze would be taken off on September 30, 1974, and that every dime raised from the export tax would go back to the owners of the resource, the provinces.
The government, in effect, said it had to do this because there was a difficult inflationary situation. What a bunch of nonsense that turned out to be. Far from being a temporary freeze, it became permanent. Far from every dime raised in export taxes being sent back to the producing provinces, nothing was sent back. Far from agreeing that the producing provinces own the resources as indicated in the British North America Act-that they have certain rights of ownership that are inherent in our common law-the government sought to take over all these prerogatives of ownership and in fact to leave the producing provinces with ownership in name only, and no authority.
Now we see Bill C-32 as one more step in the same direction. What has happened in the oil and gas industry as a result of this activity? Today, exploration and development has dropped off markedly. We are the only petrolific country in the world which has a reduction in exploration and development activity. We are losing personnel and equipment. We need exploration and development in order to supply Canada's needs. We face shortages of natural gas and oil in three years and six years, respectively. We have an industry which previously was very optimistic and is now very despondent. Companies which had great exploration and development programs are now laying off and transferring workers. As a member from that area, it is difficult for me not to react at least somewhat angrily when I find that friends and acquaintances of long-standing, loyal Canadians who like Calgary and want to live and raise their families there, are now in a position where in order to pursue their occupation they must move to Dallas, the Middle East, Indonesia or Australia.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are a few matters that I want to raise in this debate on Bill C-32. I shall begin by attempting to explain the situation to hon. members who do not come from regions where petroleum is produced. I am speaking here not simply of provinces or of cities but of rural areas where people rely for their livelihood and sustenance upon the oil industry. These people often come from other parts of the country to settle in communities which they anticipated would have some capacity to exist and where they could continue contributing to the economy and the future of Canada. A very real alarm has set in in those communities, a corrosive, cancerous alarm about the very future of their towns and their livelihoods. This matter is related directly to the bill before us, which is seen as one more instance of the

April 15, 1975
Oil and Petroleum
federal government's squeeze upon the people and the industry in this region.
I want to communicate this feeling as effectively as I can. The response is not a regional anger of westerners at the east. The response is a much more direct and personal concern about what will happen to homes, to friends, to investments and to small communities-and I know that many of my colleagues on the government side come from small communities where people have relied upon there being a sense of continuity. In many of the oil producing regions in my constituency of Rocky Mountain, which include the Pembina field and also the original Turner Valley field in Alberta, particularly in the areas where there has been active production, there exists now a sense of pessimism that I do not think has been seen in that part of the country since the days of the depression. People came there with high hopes, perhaps no higher than those of people who moved to other communities to start their careers, but they have seen those hopes suddenly undermined and they are naturally concerned.
Already, in towns such as Drayton Valley, Whitecourt, Fox Creek and Swan Hills-communities that might mean nothing to some hon. members here but which mean a great deal to those who live in them-there is a great and growing concern about the number of people who have moved away, leading businessmen in the towns who ran the Scout groups, who served on municipal councils and school boards, people who saw their businesses in oil field servicing dry up or suddenly become so uneconomical that they unloaded them at a loss. These people are facing problems that are not simply personal but problems that strike at the life of the community.
This is one of the consequences of Bill C-32 and the family of acts of intervention of which this bill is a part. If there were anything inevitable about this, perhaps we would simply have to accept it. I think that no one here is attempting to maintain communities artificially at the standard they had previously. But the point I want to make and what causes so much concern, frustration and bewilderment among constituents of mine is that this attack on the communities where oil and petroleum is produced is not necessary at all. There is no reason for it to happen. The reserves of petroleum and of natural gas in those areas are sufficiently high to allow the communities to expect a long, natural lifespan.
What is shortening that lifespan, what is bringing concern and the possibility of attrition to those communities is not any natural force. It is-and I say this deliberately and precisely-the actions of this government as embodied in Bill C-32, the unilateral introduction of the export tax and of other actions which have been taken without any kind of consideration for the human and social effects which they will have upon parts of the country.
I said that the major concern of the oil producing communities such as those I have enumerated has to do with the immediate effect upon the community of the decisions of the government. There are many businessmen who two or three years ago thought that things were good, that they would be able to provide for their families and prepare for their future, but who are now having second thoughts. There is that level of concern about the immediate future of the community.

A matter which should receive careful attention from the House-even if there is not much compassion on the government side for individuals in the communities in my constituency-is the effect that this kind of action has upon the attachment to this country of people who are as good and productive as any whom hon. members opposite have in their constituencies. They see the accumulation of federal initiatives in the energy field as initiatives directed, not against the Premier of Alberta whom the minister might lampoon as some kind of sheik, but against themselves, against their region, against their aspirations.
There has suddenly been a movement directly into their homes, into their lives, of a kind of attack from Ottawa. Naturally, if you see all around you evidence that the direction of the Government of Canada is clearly and precisely against your interest in ways that you can quantify, such as in the number of rigs that leave town, or businesses that begin to lay off their employees or delay expansion, then you begin to wonder about the cost and value of your commitment to the country of which you have always been proud.
I think it would be foolish if members on the government side looked upon the series of acts taken by the minister and his colleagues in energy matters as simply having to do with energy, because in fact they have to do much more with the capacity of the country to hold together and with the will of the people in my part of the country to remain active and contributing Canadians. I had the opportunity the other day to take my colleague, the hon. member for Don Valley, the energy critic of the official opposition, to one of those communities, to Drayton Valley, to see for himself some of the operations in the field and to talk to some of the people who live there in an atmosphere of uncertainty that would worry any member of the House if he found it in his constituency.
The hon. member for Don Valley went away with a predominant understanding, which he had not been able to learn from books or even from elevating debates in the House, of the degree of pride that people who work in the oil industry take in the work they are doing. They consider themselves to be producing Canadians who are dedicating their lives to building the country and to making it grow. They are absolutely bewildered, and indeed their faith in Canada is shattered, when they see a series of government actions which in accumulation seem to attack them for doing the very thing in which they have taken so much pride.
I should say in passing-and I note that the minister is here-that many of the people whom we met in the oil fields in Drayton Valley expressed to the hon. member for Don Valley not simply their appreciation of the fact that he had come to see for himself the human side of what was being done by Ottawa, but also the hope that the minister himself would come. They had hoped that the minister would remove himself from the protection of his advisers who perhaps see things in terms of war games with the provinces or, indeed, perhaps in terms of war games with OPEC nations, and would come himself to visit the people who work and live in an area of Canada where petroleum is produced and where the confidence in an ability to carry on has been very seriously undermined by the
April 15, 1975

cumulative actions of this government, of which the bill we are considering is only one.
Other members of the House of Commons who have participated in this debate have raised questions about the constitution and about the reason the Government of Canada is embarking upon this particular instrument to try to achieve the goal it says it needs this bill to achieve. I think it is fair for hon. members to be frank with one another. My suspicion is that the real motive for this bill and for the other actions of which it has been part is not a concern about achieving an immediate consensus on price, nor is it a concern about establishing a particular price level in the country; it is, instead, a concern to accumulate to the bosom of the federal government as much power as it possibly can.
As others have argued and as I intend to argue later today, there is no need for this particular instrument to accomplish the goals which the government says it wants to accomplish. Those goals can be accomplished by other means. There is an extraordinary emergency power already in the constitution. There is the well established practice, venerated through many years of Canadian experience, of working out agreements on matters which cause disagreement between the provinces in conferences such as the one we saw last week. There are a number of other ways of doing this; but the only instrument the government is prepared to choose is one which will aggrandize its own power-and I think that that is rooted, unhappily, in a very dangerous view held by the government of the nature of this country.
I regretted yesterday, when the Prime Minister was uttering a very well deserved tribute to the late Senator Crerar-I have not checked to see if the "blues" were corrected-that he made a point of saying that Senator Crerar, when he spoke for western Canada, did not speak in negative terms of alienation or diversity. That, surely, is the operative word. Perhaps he meant "division." I will give him the benefit of the doubt and say that perhaps he meant "division". But if he meant diversity-and I believe that is the word Hansard shows in relation to his comments on the late Senator Crerar-that indicates a highly dangerous attitude in this country. It indicates a fundamental suspicion of diversity. In my view and in the view of others who come from other parts of the country, whether they are from areas like Cape Breton, where there are continuing attempts against great odds to maintain culture and civilization and to mine coal, or whether they come from western Alberta, we realize the tremendous importance in this country of national policy which reflects diversity.
We realize, too, that the federal system we have is not a system imposed by someone else from a distance or for some theoretical reason. It is a system which developed because it is the only system which could work in a country so broad and diverse but which wanted to haul together. What frightens me about the attitude I see on the part of this government as it reaches out to establish power under its own control-whether by establishing Petro-Canada or by introducing Bill C-32 which gives it a power it does not need, or by other actions-is that it is trying to change the balance of confederation and to
Oil and Petroleum
reduce the capacity of provinces and regions which reflect the peculiar diversity of their areas to have that diversity reflected in the whole country.
Quite apart from other questions which might arise in connection with Bill C-32, there is no question-anyone who comes from a distant part of the country will agree with this-that a decision taken here in the isolation of Ottawa respecting other parts of the country will not be taken intelligently unless there is some direct contact with those other parts of the country. The way we can now assure some degree of consultation and of reflection of the great diversity of this country is by having a federal system which is federal in fact and which allows various provinces to exercise powers which are important to them.
This is not a question strictly of economics or energy because, as I indicated at the beginning of my remarks, the effects of this initiative and others which are most notable to me, as a member of parliament who goes home to his constituency, are not the economic or direct energy effects; they are the social effects and the disruption of communities whose leaders must move or operate in uncertainty; they are the effects upon the willingness to remain active in contributing parts of Canada; and they are the effects we see upon the pride which has existed to this point in energy producing areas of this country.
What worries me most of all about this bill is that it is a symbol and a symptom of a much broader attitude toward the nature of a country which considers diversity to be a danger, and which believes that the only way we can achieve agreement in this country is by giving the federal government a big enough club to beat the provinces or regions into some kind of submission. That suggestion is a highly dangerous principle upon which to proceed in a country.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton, quoting his leader, says that this is a bunch of crap. Well, I agree with him in so far as following that philosophy is a bunch of crap if we want to hold Canada together. But I challenge him to explain to me what other kinds of motives are generating the policies of the government which here, in Bill C-32, is trying to secure an extraordinary power which it does not need; which is determined, under the Petro-Canada bill, to set up an agency whose primary purpose is simply to add to the armament of the federal government; which is acting, in the courts of Canada, to stop the development of cable television and of a cable capacity in the provinces, and which is working in various other fields to aggrandize its own power and to weaken the power of the regions of Canada-because if that philosophy is followed, it could lead to the destruction of the country. I am afraid that it is a philosophy which is all too evident in this bill, because under it the Government of Canada will have an extraordinary power which it does not need. The government can, in extreme circumstances or in emergencies, exercise this power under the provisions already in the constitution. I think that power is the motive and it is a highly dangerous motive.
There is another aspect of this question of the acquisition by the government of extraordinary power. When the

April 15, 1975
Oil and Petroleum
partners in confederation, the provinces and the national government, come to the table more or less as equals, there is an onus upon them to agree. They know that if they do not agree there will be no agreement, bqt when an extraordinary club or an extraordinary power is put into the hands of one of the members at that table, that undermines the determination of the other partners to come to agreement. It corrodes and erodes the willingness to negotiate. If we grant this desire, we are going to take away from the premiers the incentive to agree when meetings are held such as the one last week. Why should they make all kinds of trade-offs in an effort to ensure the continuity of this country, if the decision is going to be imposed anyway? There is no point in negotiating with a government which already has the power to do what it wants to do.
This instrument would allow the government, whatever the issue, whatever sides people were taking on questions relating to energy, to go to a negotiating table without the need to negotiate. That would undermine the whole future and capacity of negotiations in this country. Anyone acquainted with the history of federal-provincial relations in Canada knows that our success and continuity as a country has relied substantially on the willingness of the various partners to negotiate. It is that willingness which would be undermined if the federal government acquired this extraordinary power.
What is being asked for in Bill C-32 is a regular, continuing, extraordinary power for the Government of Canada; a power which it does not have today. If it did have it in this form, we would not need this law. The government is trying to put into law a new, extraordinary power.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the bill before us there are three things which must be considered. The first is the question of unity within this country and the whole subject of federal-provincial relations. The second thing is security of supply of energy for Canada in the foreseeable and distant future. The third important thing is the question of industrial development in western Canada. I think it is fair to say that in the past three, four or five years of this government these three considerations have been in danger.
I should first like to deal briefly with the question of unity. We can all remember the good old days when previous federal governments paid some attention to the constitution of this country and made genuine efforts to maintain reasonable working relationships with the provincial governments. In the last couple of years in particular, steps have been taken by this government, particularly through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, which have put a strain on federal-provincial relationships.
Less than two years ago there was a sudden increase in the world price of petroleum. At that time the federal government, without consultation with the governments of the producing provinces, and in their usual practice of

government by news release, announced a tax on all petroleum products exported from this country. I do not object to the principle of the tax or what it was intended to do, but I do object to running roughshod over federal-provincial relations. This attitude cannot be tolerated in our country where so much depends upon unity and good relations between the provincial governments and the federal government.
The next step the government took was to introduce the energy allocations bill. This piece of legislation called for an inordinate amount of power to be given to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; power far beyond what could conceivably be required to deal with any emergency. This measure was introduced without meaningful consultation with the producing provinces and was pushed through in the manner of the playground bully.
The government then imposed the budgetary provision which eliminated royalties from income tax deductibility. That not only created a strain on federal-provincial relations but it created instability in the industry and the economy. The government has followed the pattern set by introducing this petroleum administration bill without meaningful consultation with the producing provinces. The bill provides, in effect, that if the producing provinces do not agree to put a suggested price on oil, then the federal government will do it. Such an attitude is not conducive to good relations.
One could easily draw the conclusion from the steps I have outlined, Mr. Chairman, that this minister wants to amass the power in his own hands, and one might ask why. Certainly, the measures I refer to, particularly the tax changes, have led to an unwillingness on the part of the petroleum industry to carry on with the job it has been doing so well in this country. The government does not seem to have learned anything from the steps it has taken; it does not seem to have observed that exploration and development is decreasing or that security of supply of energy products is jeopardized. It continues to ride roughshod over everybody in order to achieve its goal.
One could almost conclude that this is a deliberate attempt to destroy the petroleum industry in order to make it easier for the federal government to take over not only energy resources but, in due course, all natural resource development in this country. It seems to me that is the direction in which the minister is heading. If the government wants to go in that direction, it should come clean with the people of Canada and say in this House what it is doing. Obviously, it is heading in that direction. Hon. friends to my left may applaud this move, but at least we know where they stand. They stand in different places on different days, but generally speaking they favour nationalizing resource industries, and they have said so.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has often said inside and outside this House that he is in favour of private enterprise developing petroleum and other natural resource industries in this country, yet his actions belie his statements. Not long ago the National Energy Board issued a report which said that
April 15, 1975

within the next eight or nine years Canadian petroleum products would be in short supply. That report shocked many Canadians because not long ago we were told that we possessed sufficient energy supplies to last us several decades, not just one. Yet suddenly we were told there would be a shortage in the near future.
One wonders about the accuracy of such reports. If there is to be a petroleum shortage within the next ten years, why does the government follow policies which discourage the development of our petroleum industry? Indeed, government policies are bringing about a decrease in exploration and are hindering development. Exploration is on the downswing and companies are looking to other parts of the world for investment. They seek to explore elsewhere because conditions in this country for them have become unpalatable.
What about quid pro quo for the West? About a year ago, when the federal government began intruding on provincial jurisdiction in the field of energy, it at least tried to console westerners. Ministers said, "We are going to skim off as much income as we can from the provinces and put it in the federal treasury, but in return we will implement policies beneficial to western development." They talked about reducing transportation costs and stimulating industrial development. We do not hear about these things any more. Nobody on the government side talks about quid pro quo for the west; the subject has been forgotten. Instead, the government is now concerned with power; it wants to invade, as quickly as possible, provincial jurisdiction and take over as quickly as possible the development of natural resources. Apparently it is not concerned with the long-term effects on security of supply.
A moment ago I said that a National Energy Board report indicates that we possess supplies of conventional petroleum sufficient only for the next eight or ten years. In the middle of my constituency and forming a large part of it exists one of the largest undeveloped deposits of petroleum in the world in the form of the Athabasca tar sands. It seems to me that development of the tar sands is essential to make sure we do not run out of petroleum by the end of the decade. I am in favour, of course, of increasing exploration for conventional oil: we must do all we can to find and develop these resources. However, we all know that supplies of conventional oil are decreasing. The only logical way to guarantee long-term security of supply for this country lies in the speedy development of the tar sands.
I am distressed to note that the government's remarkable vacillations in policy regarding this country's petroleum industry have resulted in a falling off of interest in the development of the tar sands. Consider for a moment the gestation period needed before a new plant can be born, so to speak. A long period must elapse between the conception of a plant on the drawing board and the actual production of oil. Obviously, we must not waste time; we must develop the tar sands. Past experience shows that it takes, on average, five years to turn a plant conceived on the drawing board into reality. It takes five years to bring new tar sands oil on stream.
At present this country consumes about two million barrels of oil a day. We export about one million barrels of western oil and import an equivalent amount to supply the
Adjournment Motion
markets of eastern Canada. As I said, the interval between the design on the drawing board and the operating plant is, on average, five years. We know that tar sands plants of a capacity of about 100,000 barrels a day are being designed. If we want to be assured of secure supplies after the end of the present decade, we must make certain that we possess at least ten tar sands plants each producing
100.000	barrels a day by that time. We need at least one million barrels a day of tar sands oil. Simple arithmetic shows we shall need ten plants each with a production of
100.000	barrels a day.
At present we are not likely to reach this production target. At the moment one plant produces about 65,000 barrels a day and another, under construction, will produce about 125,000 barrels per day. Two or three plants are in the early planning stages and may or may not go ahead. We do not know if they will proceed. This government's vacillating policies have caused uncertainty in the industry and have proved a deterrent to people who want to develop the tar sands. The government should not deter such people; it ought to be concerned about security of supply. We know what could happen if this country became more dependent than it is today on offshore supplies of oil. Oil prices are unpredictable, Madam Chairman.
May I call it five o'clock?

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the comments made by the chief government whip, but I wish to point out that the order of business is not completely in the hands of the House leaders. There is an order paper. At five o'clock on Tuesday the order is private members' business. We would be perfectly within our right to say we will take the first item and then the second item, whether members know about it or not. However, when it is clearly understood that a bill that is called will take only two or three minutes, there should be an understanding that we will move on to something else. I just say it is something we could do.
If we reach the point where there is nothing we can do, I make the same plea I made the last time. This hour, which

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, just before the committee recessed I was saying that the country in which we live has been severely damaged by the policies of the government. I said it was damaged in three ways. The first was in the area of federal-provincial relations and general unity. I said this damage had been done because no consultations of a meaningful nature had taken place before the
Oil and Petroleum
announcement of major policies on energy matters was made by the minister.
I also said the country had been damaged as a result of the instability surrounding the petroleum industry, an insecurity which jeopardized the security of future supply. The most obvious place at which the effects of this instability are now visible is the development of the Athabasca tar sands. It is estimated that by the end of the present decade we shall require a million barrels or so a day from the sands, and to achieve this level ten plants must be constructed before the end of the next ten-year period, each producing some 100,000 barrels a day. Because of the time it takes for a plant to go on stream, some five years, it is evident we are up against what I would consider to be an emergency situation right now. Steps must be taken very soon to stimulate the industry, to create a feeling of well-being in the economy so that this important development can proceed forthwith.
I realize it is becoming increasingly popular to expect governments to participate to an ever greater extent in the development of natural resources, particularly in the field of energy. We also are aware that no governments have the machinery or the know-how at the moment to take over from private enterprise-I do not say they could not get it, but at the moment they do not have it. I am not arguing now that government should take over from private enterprise; all I am saying is that private enterprise has been working in this area for several decades and doing a good job. It is only since there has been marked interference on the part of the federal government, and maybe some others, that supplies have been in jeopardy. While some members of the House, and some people in the country may daydream about the day when governments are completely responsible for energy production, the fact remains that our only hope at the moment of assuring security of supply within the next decade or so lies in encouraging the people who have proven their success in the past, and who already have the know-how and the required machinery. I want to impress this on the mind of the minister in the hope he will give it some thought and take steps which will be more useful than those he has taken so far.
This is not the time, Madam Chairman, to be taunting the provinces, or picking fights with the various regions of the country. In days in which Canada is threatened by unemployment on one hand and inflation on the other, the federal government should be striving for co-operation and taking a conciliatory approach in an effort to solve collectively the serious problems which beset the nation. We have not seen this happening. Instead, particularly as far as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is concerned, we have witnessed a series of confrontations staged for no particular reason. It is important that this situation be changed. Perhaps the Prime Minister himself should take a more active role in this area. The Prime Minister is probably quite sincere when he says he wants to come to grips with inflation in some way; his efforts so far have not resulted in any significant improvement. I should like to see the Prime Minister go down in history as the man who, to use his own phrase, wrestled inflation to the ground. However, I fear history will record of his leadership only the phrase "Pierre fuddled while Canada burned".

April 15, 1975
Oil and Petroleum

Madam Chairman, in approaching legislation such as Bill C-32 I am surprised the government, when considering the implications, did not see fit to make a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada. It is not as though there was not sufficient time to permit this to be done-as a number of hon. members have mentioned, this particular piece of legislation has been before the House for many months. The regulation of trade and commerce has always been a delicate and controversial subject. The bill before us has great potential for abuse by a government which is overly concerned about legislative expediency and somewhat impatient with the rights of provinces, and, indeed, of individuals.
The other day I was looking at a book by a contemporary authority on the Canadian constitution, W. R. Leder-man, a very distinguished academic who at one time was at Dalhousie University when I was studying there. This distinguished gentleman had some very interesting things to say about the role of courts generally in relation to our constitution, and I should like to put on the record some brief excerpts from his book, which is entitled "The Courts and the Canadian Constitution". Professor Leder-man makes the point that the court has an educational role to play, and at page 172 of this book we find the following:
It is well recognized that the ultimate court in a federal system plays two roles in relation to public opinion. It is first the institutional symbol of balance in the national life, the instrument which seeks to preserve unity in the system of diversity of interest and legal power involved in federalism. Secondly, its deliverances help to educate the public mind as to the historic purposes of the constitution, and the principles applied in the determination of great internal issues.
I do not think any of us would seriously question that under present circumstances this is a great internal issue. A determination is being made by this highest court in the land, parliament, of what the historic role of the provinces will be in the future, having regard to the rights that they and their people have to deal with their own natural resources. The Supreme Court of Canada should have a role as well. Professor Lederman goes on to say that the court is an umpire of the federal system. May I return here to the point with which I began these few remarks and suggest to the minister that I am surprised he did not seek to make use of our Supreme Court.
Professor Lederman continues:
It is the prime function of the final court to keep the exercise of legislative powers by parliament or legislatures within the limits marked out for them. For that purpose it must interpret the heads of jurisdiction relevant to each exercise of asserted legislative power in reaching its conclusion of validity or invalidity.
