speechtext:
As the hon. member for Peace River says, the minister made reference to the fact that he had received the benefit of an opinion from the Minister of Justice. I believe his exact words were that the bill being put forward carries with it the judgment of the Department of Justice that it is, indeed, within the legislative power of the parliament of Canada to pass this particular

enactment. I say to the minister in all sincerity, how much better would it be if he were able to make that statement with reference to the Supreme Court of Canada; and I say that with all due deference to the Minister of Justice.
In looking at another major act dealing with energy, the act that set up the National Energy Board and which came into effect in 1959, it was never intended by that piece of legislation to give the federal government the right to come into a province and fix the wellhead price for petroleum products. The government of that the day exhibited, albeit under circumstances quite different, though not entirely so, from those existing today, a more commendable concern for the rights of the provinces and the citizens of the provinces, since at that particular time the government was content, through the board, by transport controls and so on, to exert an impact on price at the place of arrival, a much different situation from moving in and interfering with prices at the source.
As other hon. members have said-and I do not wish to belabour the point-by applying the same reasoning as that applied to petroleum products the government could institute controls on the price of lumber, because most provinces export lumber. It could do it with iron ore because iron ore will eventually become steel and might be exported. No resource is exempt. So it is quite clear that the government has, if it so chooses, the power to change drastically the traditional roles that the provinces have played in managing their own resources ever since confederation.
I repeat that it becomes imperative that the government do what it did about a year ago, namely, use every effort to bring the provincial premiers back again in a more subdued and businesslike attitude to achieve a consensus, without resorting to legislative enactments of this sort. Again I caution the minister to avoid his tendency to be impatient and inflexible because of his understandable concern to achieve his objective.
There is another option that the minister and his colleagues should pursue to the utmost extent. I refer to bilateral discussions between the producing provinces and the federal government in an attempt to achieve written agreements, preferably supplemented by statutory provisions. If there really is a crisis in the area of Energy, as it was claimed there was about a year ago but which has since turned out to be considerably less than a crisis, if surely, the government can act, as it did with the Energy Allocation Act, as if there were a genuine state of emergency and deal with the situation, without being at this time in a great rush to enact this particular piece of legislation.
A province like Alberta, or any other province for that matter, cannot realistically make an agreement to sell petroleum products outside its own borders without the co-operation of the consuming provinces and the federal government agencies concerned with the transportation of such products. Given the co-operative nature of the marketing and transportation process, I want to ask the minister, without going into the many arguments previously cited, why the matter was not referred to the Supreme Court of Canada so that this, our highest and most prestigious court, could have formulated, through its ruling, the legal and constitutional position.
April 15, 1975

This ruling could then have served not only as a guide to Parliament and to the government in proceeding with its legislation; it would have demonstrated to all Canadians, and particularly to all those having the responsibility to govern in provinces, that the federal government was truly concerned with the rule of law and was using the resources of our Supreme Court to assist in evolving legislation which, by its very subject matter, had fundamental constitutional implications.
I did not intend to cite a possible amendment in its entirety at this stage, but it does seem to me that it would be appropriate to move an amendment at the end of the bill. For example, an amendment could be moved to add immediately following clause 95 on page 39 a new clause, which could be clause 96, providing for reference to the Supreme Court. Such an amendment could read as follows:
(1)	Forthwith after this act is assented to in Her Majesty's name, the governor in council, under section 55 of the Supreme Court Act, shall refer all questions of law and fact concerning the constitutionality of this act and every provision thereof other than this section to the Supreme Court.
(2)	Until the Supreme Court has certified to the governor in council its opinion upon each such question, no provision of this act, other than this section, shall come into force at the time of commencement provided therefor under this act or the Interpretation Act and then only to the extent, if any, such provision is in the opinion of the court within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada.
I think that is necessary in view of clauses 52 and 35, which provide that they come into effect upon proclamation. Another subclause could be added to this effect:
(3)	The attorney general of each province shall be notified of the hearing under this section in order that he may be heard if he thinks fit.
I have tried to be reasonably specific in what I have said this evening, that is to say, I have registered my concern about why the resources of the Supreme Court have not in fact been utilized by the minister and the government, since they are there and presumably are available to give guidance. I want to conclude by saying that I hope the minister will address himself to this point and provide me with a resume of why he has not taken this sort of action. Perhaps he will also say whether he feels that what I have suggested has any merit or not.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, the reason I did not rise in more of a rush was that I thought the minister would wish to respond to the comments made by the hon. member for Central Nova. This petroleum administration legislation, I believe, does a very good job of setting out the philosophy of the government which governs Canada at the present time. It is the philosophy of confrontation.
When the government cannot achieve its purpose through the proper channels it is more than willing to bring out a club with which literally to ram its feelings down the throats of the objectors. It is no wonder there was not agreement reached at the recent conference of
Oil and Petroleum
first ministers. How could our provincial administrations be assured that the federal government would not do exactly what it did after the previous meeting? Shortly after that meeting it introduced a budget which, to my understanding, was in disagreement with the consensus reached, and by which it no longer allowed royalties to be an expense deduction.
I should like to read briefly the reaction of the petroleum industry to the elimination of the expense deduction. It reads as follows:
The petroleum industry has been swift and bitterly critical in its reaction to federal budget proposals that may take as much as $800 million away from it in a full year.
Industry men said they deplored the fact that Ottawa has failed to heed earlier complaints that if the tax proposals-first put out in the defeated federal budget of last May-were passed, producers could face an economically untenable position.
I am as concerned about the petroleum industry as about the small consumer, because if we do not have exploration by our petroleum industries we will not have the supply to give to the individuals who so badly need it, and our concern must be a surety of supply.
I wish also to take a few moments to compare this federal administration to the government of Alberta and its reaction. Alberta somehow feels it is just coming into its own in regard to confederation, but the present federal administration wishes to continue its policy of excluding the western parts of our country from full participation in confederation. As I stated earlier, I should like to compare the attitude of the federal government to the attitude of the provincial government of Alberta. I shall quote out of context some remarks made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources when he spoke to the Science Teachers Association of Ontario on November 16, 1974. He stated:
I say ... the principles of our policy, and they are threefold in regard to petroleum: To reach, through consultation with the provinces, a phased increase in the price of crude oil to a level sufficient to bring on the required additional supplies for Canadians without jumping to the high levels set by the OPEC group;...
I should like to dwell on his statement in respect of consultation with the provinces. With regard to this bill, is the minister willing to take the advice and guidance of the provinces when the bill contains a veto clause? What type of consultation is that? This is not consultation, but confrontation. Again let me stress that this administration wishes to have a club by which it can beat and mold the provinces to its own federal wishes.
As a comparison I should like to read the statement of Premier Lougheed which he gave at the federal-provincial conference in Ottawa on January 22, 1974. He stated:
Alberta welcomes the opportunity to participate in this federal-provincial conference on energy. As the major supplier of energy for Canada, we obviously have a substantial stake in the development of sound and fair national energy policies. They must be national policies though-national in the sense they are developed by agreement between the federal government and the provinces and with full recognition that natural resources located within the provinces, under our constitution, are owned by the provinces.
The Premier of Alberta states, "they must be national policies". By his past experience I believe he has proved he is willing to respect the national interest. As he says in his statement, with which I am in agreement, the resources are the property of the provinces under our constitution.

April 15, 1975
Oil and Petroleum
At the same time we find that this Liberal administration is not willing to abide by our constitution and recognize the fact that resources are the property of the provinces. The federal government is not willing to heed the constitution and the rights of the provinces. It is more inclined to ram its beliefs down the throats of what might appear to be minor governments.
There are many areas in respect of petroleum in which we should be very interested. I feel they are somewhat overlooked by this government because it is more interested in grabbing the wealth these resources will produce. The two areas on which I wish to dwell specifically are supply and national unity. The National Energy Board states that Canada will lose its self-sufficiency in respect to oil production by 1982 even if oil exports to the United States are cut off. What has the minister done in the area of security of our supply? What is he doing in respect of finding future reserves which will be very much in demand by future generations? I do not believe he is doing anything in this regard, or in respect of national unity, although the government suggests it is doing much to foster this cause.
I should like to refer to a few paragraphs from an editorial appearing in the Edmonton Journal of November 30, 1974, in respect to national unity. I believe it is very appropriate to discuss national unity with regard to this bill because I have a strong inner feeling that the present federal administration thrives on confrontation. It believes in dividing this country as much as it can, and then appearing as the godfather who can bring our country back together again with national unity policies, even when it is the parent that fostered the disgruntled feelings that exist throughout our nation. The editorial states:
In 1865, when the Eighth Provincial Parliament of Canada asked Queen Victoria to allow the formation of a federation of provinces in British North America, the central objective was 'to protect the diversified interest of the several provinces, and secure efficiency, harmony, and permanency in the Union.'
This government has done very little to protect the diversified interests of the many regions of our country simply because all it does is to appeal to the populace which will continue to re-elect it. The article goes on to say:
On the surface, the dispute between Ottawa and Alberta is a simple political dogfight over wealth and who will control it. If the conflict were indeed a limited wrangle over money it would be relatively easy to resolve. Instead, profound questions about national unity and the kind of Canada we will have in the future are emerging from the debate.
I think the situation is extremely touchy when we have various regions in Canada competing against each other because the government is dividing us to such an extent that we will be more concerned about regional interests than about the national interest of our country.
The article goes on to read:
Ottawa has challenged the provinces' traditionally accepted right to certain benefits accruing from ownership and development of natural resources...
The federal government is challenging these rights in the bill before us. It would not be so bad if it challenged these rights from time to time, but it is its arrogant
[Mr. Elzinga.)
attitude in challenging provinces such as Alberta, which produces 85 per cent of the oil in our country, that is so unacceptable. I think we are all aware that what we do want is only a fair price. We do not want to be used as puppets on a string by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
The editorial also states:
What is alarming about the Alberta case is that Ottawa's approach to oil pricing and resource royalties embodies the concept of a confederation in which provincial jurisdictions can be invaded unilaterally, both in spirit and in fact, at the whim of the central government; a confederation in which the provinces are entirely subservient to the federal authority and are, in effect, political adjuncts to the federal power.
That is just what this bill will do to the provinces, and that is why we in the Conservative party cannot agree with it. It is our hope that the minister will agree to amend the bill to include a provision for consultation with the provinces and to exclude a veto clause under which the government could force its own wishes on individual provinces across the country.
The article also states:
It is equally ironic that Prime Minister Trudeau, that most articulate and ardent supporter of Canadian federalism, should be heading the government that is sowing such discord among the provinces.
Let me state, incidentally, that I disagree with the statement in the article that the Prime Minister is an articulate and ardent supporter of Canadian federalism. It is evident that the government thrives on confrontation and this bill is a fine example of just that.
I should like to relate to the committee a story that was told to me a good many years ago. As it comes back to my mind it makes me think of our present administration and of our Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. It is a story about a man who envisioned himself pushing a wheelbarrow with a man sitting in it, on a tightrope across Niagara Falls. What our minister is asking of the Canadian people is for them to hop into a wheelbarrow which he would push on a tightrope across Niagara Falls.
I think it is evident that in western Canada we do not have that much faith in this administration, and rightly so, judging from the administration's past actions. For example, an agreement was reached by this government and the provinces a year ago but subsequently disregarded in the budget. How can we have faith in an administration that agrees to one thing at one time, and rejects it when it no longer fits its purpose?
In conclusion I should like to pose the same question that the hon. member for Central Nova put to the minister, because I am very interested in the minister's reaction to that proposal put forward by the hon. member. I would also like to know the reaction this government has received to this legislation from the various provinces.

As a matter of fact this bill affects
April 15, 1975

all parts of Canada, and particularly the province of Ontario.
It is important that we consider for a moment the geography of this country and, if one does so, one realizes that in terms of access to supply of energy, whether for home consumption for the operation of automobiles or for the operation and fueling of the industrial capacity of central Canada-which I know is sometimes the cause of comment in other parts of Canada-petroleum is significant, and Ontario is a land locked province. Any discussions in this House, any first ministers' conference, any statements by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on any aspect dealing with the supply of energy for all of the purposes I have mentioned do not end, so far as we are concerned, at the Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba borders but they concern us also deeply and vitally in this part of Canada.
So I think that we must look at this bill from the point of view of Ontario, and the first question we must ask of the minister is: what will this bill do under the present circumstances to ensure one more gallon of oil, one more cubic foot of natural gas, that could not be provided by reasonable consultation? I do not want any member of the House to think that the only people who are concerned about the proper interpretation of this badly battered British North America Act are the people of Alberta or the people of western Canada, because we in central Canada are very much concerned as well.
From the point of view of central Canada the significance of the first ministers' conference and of the proposed legislation, as well as all that flows from those two events, and indeed of the attitude of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, is that if the power is given to the minister and to his department as set forth in clauses 36 and 52, then the people of central Canada can expect forthwith an increase in the price of fuel, in the price of gas, and in other prices.

speechtext:
That is how important this is to the province of Ontario, and it is precisely for this reason, and also because there is a deep constitutional matter involved in this whole consideration, that the premier of Ontario, the Hon. William Davis, took the position which he was bound to take at the first ministers' conference last week. I think it is important that the people of Ontario, and the hon. members from Ontario on the other side of the House who represent people in Ontario, understand the importance of that position.
I heard the speech made by the premier of Ontario. In a statistical way he outlined what an increase in the price of oil might mean immediately. He told of the effect it could have on inflation, on employment, and on the development
Oil and Petroleum
of industry in the province of Ontario. It is important to Canada, just as it is important to all of us in Ontario and in any other part of Canada, that there be a reasonable opportunity for the continuance and development of the petroleum industry in western Canada.
Surely the essence of this debate is the balance of interest between the various provinces of Canada. When the minister, in the absence of a crisis, takes upon himself the powers this bill gives to him, or he asks this parliament to give to him, then I think anyone who has any feeling at all about this question of the constitutional balance between the provinces and the central government has to sit up and take notice, and ask why and what the effect of it will be.
I certainly would agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain who said, in effect, that the whole constitutional process of this country has been one of consultation. I think this is one of the few times when there has been an attempt by the federal government to amend by a statute the British North America Act, and it is really an attempt to do indirectly what it could not do directly. There is not one member of parliament or anyone in the country who would say, given a demonstrable crisis or an emergency, that the government ought not to have the powers it asks for, but there are very few people in this country who, in the absence of that emergency or crisis, would willingly allow this unilateral amendment to the British North America Act. The leader of the government has indicated that if he is given this power-and that is why he is asking for it-he is going to raise the price of petroleum. That is not to say that the price of petroleum ought to stay the same forever. Of course it cannot.
There is something unique about this country. The constitution of this country came about because some fairly wise men in 1867 decided that it was worth while to build a nation in the northern half of North America. Given the state of affairs and the threats they were confronted with at that time, and the advantages which would accrue to nationhood, they sat around a table, consulted, came to an agreement, and the country was born. It is a pretty fragile thing, a country born out of agreement and consensus rather than revolution and war. That fragility has to be nurtured at each turn of the road, and this government is about as far removed from the good constitutional gardener as I can imagine.
There have been some in my part of Canada who have called the premier of Alberta a blue eyed Arab, and a number of other things. Much of this has emanated from the press. Much has emanated from the mouths of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In all of this they have perhaps done more damage to the cause of confederation than anything else.
I have listened very carefully to the speeches which have been made, I have read the reports and the statements, and I think that it has to be recognized that a provincial premier has a legitimate part to play in the national scene, and that, if he failed to play his part, most Canadians in his province would repudiate him. I think that the premier of Alberta adopted at the conference a reasonable attitude with respect to this situation, having regard to his interest and the national interest. It is that kind of attitude of reasonableness which ought to be

April 15, 1975
Oil and Petroleum
seized upon by the government rather than immediately legislating into place the power the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources just loves to wield. Perhaps an element of understanding, which even he may be capable of from time to time, should be wheeled into place.
It has to be demonstrated to this House that all consultation has failed at the time that agreements run out, that there is indeed a crisis in terms of supply, that there is a difficulty with respect to the development industries- those things must be balanced-and if there were a referral to this parliament of that situation then I am satisfied that this parliament would react in the national interest, and that would be understood by the people of every province.
The BNA Act does not just sit on the statute books to be ignored or to be circumvented. This problem is so important that the minister ought to accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Central Nova and refer this matter to the Supreme Court of Canada to have the constitutional position satisfied. The minister said yesterday that he was basing his case on the regulation of interprovincial commerce. That is his whole case. He puts upon himself the clothing of a constitutional lawyer, aided and abetted by a questionable opinion from the Department of Justice. Others in the constitutional debate say that that is not so, and that it deals basically in the field of property and civil rights. It seems to me that the issues are very clearly defined. They are the kind of issues, in terms of jurisdiction, which ought to be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada. It may be that the reason why the minister is not referring it to the Supreme Court of Canada is because of some doubt about what might be the outcome.
In any event I think it is worthwhile, not just for the idle fighting of a case in court but to establish the constitutional position, that the minister consider very carefully the suggestion of the hon. member and of others, that the issues are just that important in terms of our constitution, that the varying provincial and regional interests are just that important in terms of our country, and that the interests of the people of the province of Ontario in terms of price must be balanced equitably and justly with the interests of the people of the province of Alberta in terms of development.
But, most of all, no one should sit idly by in this chamber and accept the word of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that he must have these powers, particularly when he and the leader of his government have indicated that they intend to use them immediately in a way which will likely be detrimental to the country as a whole. I ask that the minister consider this point of view. It is not just a western problem, it is not just a problem of the producing provinces, but also a problem which affects consuming provinces. I ask him to consider very carefully whether it is wise, in all of the circumstances, for him to proceed along the lines he is proceeding, in view of the importance of this issue.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I rise to intervene in this debate because I was astounded on a number of occasions, yesterday and today, by the remarks of various hon. members, particularly those to my right, and most particularly the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands has reminded me that these are the same people who were proposing price controls a short time ago. We have not heard much about that in recent months. Now we are getting it from the other side as well, and they won an election opposing price controls.
We supported this legislation on second reading on the grounds that the Government of Canada should have the power to control these prices, or to set them if agreement cannot be reached. We have also taken the position that there is absolutely no justification for oil price increases unless all the extra money derived therefrom goes into exploration and development production. If that is not the
April 15, 1975

case, then there is no legitimate reason for a price increase.
I understand why my colleagues to my right and some other people in the country feel sorry for the oil industry, but I do not agree with them. It was the premier of an oil-producing province-not the premier of Ontario or Quebec-who said that if there is to be any increase in the price of oil it should go into an energy security fund to be controlled by the people of Canada through the federal and provincial governments.
The minister has no assurance, nor have my hon. friends to my right, that the oil industry will do any more exploration than it is doing at present. One could assume, perhaps with a degree of certainty, that it would put some money into exploration, but unless all the money is allocated to exploration, development and production of energy resources, whether oil, gas, uranium, electrical power or whatever, then there is no justification for an increase. We agree, however, that in the final analysis if there is no agreement then the federal government should have that power.
I can understand why there is no agreement from at least one producing province. There was an agreement in March of last year and Saskatchewan lived up to it. Every nickel of its windfall money went into a capital fund, as had been agreed. It would have been nice, of course, to spend that money on roads, or on health and welfare, but it all went into a capital fund to be used for exploration and development. But this minister, the Minister of Finance, and the government doublecrossed us. I have urged the premier of Saskatchewan to keep his back to the wall and his gun loose in his holster the next time he comes to Ottawa, and to make sure that he gets everything in writing. In spite of that betrayal, however, the premier of Saskatchewan was the only one who returned here last week with a positive proposal.
Last night the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain said that Saskatchewan says it can steal and Alberta says it can steal. I do not know about Alberta, but the premier of Saskatchewan said that we will not steal and that, even though the resources are ours, if there is a price increase all this money will go into energy research development and exploration development.
It seems to me that a lot of this debate is not concerned so much with the constitution of Canada or the security of energy resources for the future as with the welfare and good order of a lot of multinational oil companies. What assurance do we have that the majors in the oil industry will use the funds derived from a price increase for production and exploration? The premier of Saskatchewan provided ample information. We have no assurance at all, and the evidence is to the contrary.
In spite of the fancy advertisements shown by Imperial Oil during the hockey games about how they are going to save us all in Canada, the evidence is to the contrary. While their profits after deduction of all expenses, taxes and royalties, were going up, they were not doing anything extra in exploration and production. From 1965 to 1974, with the exception of one year, their net profits from Alberta and Saskatchewan increased. In 1966 they took out of Alberta and Saskatchewan $160 million in net profits, and by 1974 they were taking $786 million. They made
Oil and Petroleum
that much after paying taxes, royalties, expenses, lifting costs-the whole bit. And what did they spend in Alberta and Saskatchewan, in 1974, for exploration and development? They spent $220 million. Where did the other $566 million go? I say that anybody who says that any amount of increased oil and gas prices should go to the industry is betraying our country and betraying the possibility of security of energy resources for the future. The companies had their chance and they blew it.

Wait; they are profits in Alberta and Saskatchewan. I am sorry. They represent oil industry profits from all over Canada. I may have been out by a few million dollars. I do not know how profits made in those provinces compare with oil profits made in the other eight provinces. Most profits were made in Alberta and Saskatchewan. I am glad the hon. member drew my attention to this fact.
The point is they made $786 million in net profits after taxes, dividends, royalties and allowing for reserves. How much did they put into exploration in all Canada, including Alberta and Saskatchewan? If you say they put $659 million into all Canada, that leaves $129 million-odd unaccounted for. Yet some people are proposing that we should raise oil prices and pay some of the increase to the industry.
Let us see what happened in the years when their cash flow was going up. What did they do in exploration? Back in 1965, 1966, 1967 and 1968, the companies made a large base profit after paying all operating expenses, including royalties, and after paying income tax, extraordinary items and discretionary expenses-whatever that means. Perhaps, in the oil industry, discretionary expenses means donations to the Liberal and Tory parties. I don't know.
Around 1965 their cash flow was in the neighbourhood of $430 million or $440 million, and the oil industry spent on exploration between $170 million and $180 million in all Canada. In Alberta and Saskatchewan they spent around $120 million. When you look at the figures for 1972-74, you will see that their cash flow was in the order of $800 million, $1,200 million and $1,600 million. Did exploration expenditures for all Canada go up proportionately? No way! They certainly did not. Their exploration expenditures went up to a total of $600 million for all Canada. Therefore the proportion is lower. Their exploration record in Alberta and Saskatchewan is even worse. The expenditure stayed where it was, in the area of $180 million to $200 million. And some people want the oil industry to get part of any increased price for oil and gas.
When the industry's cash flow climbed to the $1,600 million mark in 1974, the proportion spent on exploration went down. Why should any part of a price increase go to the industry? Some say some or all of any increase should

April 15, 1975
Oil and Petroleum
go to the industry. Really, Madam Chairman, I find that difficult to accept.
We agree that the minister should have this power if he does not get agreement. I agree with what some hon. friends to my right have said. There is good reason for at least one province, after the double-cross of last year, to say, "Bring in your budget, and we will see what we shall do. We are not prepared to make the kind of agreement we made last time. We are not prepared to play a game in which the rules change half way through it, because that is what the government did last time." The government wonders why it has difficulty getting a consensus. It will find it difficult to get any consensus even on the time of day after what happened in its dealings with certain provinces.
We hear a lot about the difficulties of independent companies, and a lot of weeping and wailing. Someone has to do the weeping and wailing for the independents, the drilling and exploration companies in Canada. Really, the big seven do not do the drilling and exploration in this country. They have done a small amount of it in the past, but the major portion of the activity has always been undertaken by independents, most of whom are Canadian-owned and who have the expertise.

Sure, companies have left Saskatchewan and Alberta. They followed the multinationals. They are the slaves of the multinational corporations, which brings me to the point about which the hon. member for Regina East is concerned. If Imperial Oil can increase its profits by 176 per cent in four years and take that much out of this country, that is not a bad deal at all. If they decide to drill in the North Sea, or Indonesia, or Nigeria, the service and drilling rigs pack up and follow them. There is nothing new about that. They have been doing it ever since the first oil well was discovered. But you do not see Imperial Oil running around with drilling service rigs; nor does any other multinational oil company do this.
The point is that in Canada we have developed expertise that is second to none in drilling, exploration, and innovation. Why do we not explore more ourselves and drill for our own oil resources? We really do not need Imperial, Gulf, Shell, Texaco, Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas, Petrofina, or Pan Canadian, the little subsidiary of the CPR. We could go ahead on our own. Even when the federal government, together with Ontario, Alberta and the Syncrude consortium made the agreement to go ahead finally with the Syncrude operation, one premier of a producing province suggested a way by which we could operate a publicly-owned Syncrude type operation. He suggested that if we put $2 per barrel on the price of oil and set that amount aside for development, each year we could spend $1.4 billion on a Syncrude-type plant. He was talking about adding a plant each year.

speechtext: And what happened in Saskatchewan in 1950?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Listen to these free enterprise supporters crying. They keep saying, "We can't do anything unless the companies do it for us." Baloney. That is a lot of malarkey, and has always been. Even the blue-eyed Arabs

of the Middle East and South America are saying that we have been "had" all these years. They say, "We don't need those oil companies," and neither do we. We have exploration and drilling expertise. True, some of the companies went bankrupt. I have some relatives who were in the oil well drilling and servicing industry and I can tell you what happened to them at the tender hands of Imperial Oil and Gulf. They invested a lifetime of savings and effort and were left in the lurch, because these multinational corporations did not do the job they were supposed to do.
Do you suppose Imperial Oil operates on principles of altruism? Why do they operate in Canada? Madam Chairman, they operated here because they wanted the bucks. That is the only reason. Their operation had nothing to do with the welfare and good order of our country and the people living in it. How much longer will we cater to these people, especially when we can do this work ourselves?
This legislation would be good if it got the minister and the government off their backsides. We could undertake these operations, either with a totally publicly-owned Crown corporation or with a combination of public ownership and private enterprise; but the operation should be Canadian-owned and controlled. That is important. The government has not had the courage to go that far. The present price of the resource appears to be the only concern of the federal government. Apparently the minister is concerned about any return that the industry needs or has the right to expect if there is to be an increase.
If the minister is going to keep using the multinational corporations and not keep on letting them use him, he needs power in the legislation to require them to put all of that extra money into research, exploration and development, not only for oil and gas, but the whole spectrum of energy sources in this country. Instead of that, he is going to go half way.
I respect the Progressive Conservative party and their concerns. At least they stand up for private enterprise and the glories of it. However, the minister wants to go down the middle and have it both ways; a little bit to industry and a little bit to the producing provinces. He wants one price for consumers across this country. He is trying to do a little bit for each of them, but is not really doing anything. It is in the same mess as it was when the Conservatives were defeated. In fact, it has got progressively worse.
I hate to say this, and I will say it without any malice. When I took my family to Montreal in 1967 to see Expo, we were happy about our one hundredth birthday and proud of confederation. However, when buying gas for my car in Ottawa, Montreal and Three Rivers, I paid between seven and ten cents a gallon less than in Saskatchewan where we live right on top of the oil. For 13 years I did not hear anyone from Ontario, Quebec or the Atlantic provinces say there should be one price across Canada. They had the benefit of cheap off-shore crude, but they did not say we should even out that price. Western Canadians paid higher gas, farm fuel and heating fuel prices for 13 years than those in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. However, we did not hear one word about there being one price across
April 15, 1975

Canada. The Middle East countries have increased their prices and eastern Canadians now have to pay more. So all of a sudden we need to have one price across Canada, and we are to have a two-price system.
Alberta and Saskatchewan have made their contribution to confederation. Both agreed to forgo hundreds of millions of dollars of revenue that could have been theirs at the world price. What happened? They got double-crossed. Saskatchewan certainly did.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I was hoping that these interesting tales from Scheherazade to which we were listening would be continued by the hon. member. However, we will get the next instalment later.
I want to comment on something that was said by the hon. member for Central Nova with regard to the question of emergency. As a matter of fact it would be rather simple for the government to establish to any intelligent and objective court that there was a state of emergency, and these powers could then be obtained. If you put before a court of this land the series of walking disasters that have been afflicted upon Canada, I am sure they would say that a country with a government like this is certainly in a state of emergency. There have been a few exceptions. The Postmaster General is now having a latter repentance about the genies he helped unloose from Pandora's box. I am mixing my metaphors, but hon. members will understand what I mean. He is trying to put them back, without too much success.
I want to ask the minister a few questions. Some are rhetorical, some are actual. He may answer them sometime during the course of the debate.
Through cases decided in the Supreme Court of Canada and by superior court judges, I have established, with the law as it now stands, that if a transaction takes place entirely within a province, it is for the province to regulate, even though the commodity is to its greatest extent being exported, or has been or will be going into the channels of interprovincial or international trade. That is the law as it has been laid down, with the following exception. If the intent of the provincial regulation or statute is clearly aimed at dealing with the regulation of trade and commerce, even though the transaction takes place entirely within the province, it is offensive and can be struck down. If that is not the case, if a transaction is entirely within a province consisting of a sale or a movement, it is for the province to regulate. The province can regulate, the federal government cannot.
In the first CalOil case a former deputy minister said that the federal government has not the right, despite clear evidence that the commodity in question was one which came from outside the country under the provisions of federal government legislation dealing with the import, subject to conditions, to have control with regard to movement from one part of the province to the other.
There was a situation in the province of Quebec where the processing and pricing of milk, which was known to be shipped out of the province to its largest extent, was squarely within the competence of the province. There
Oil and Petroleum
was a case in Saskatchewan where, despite the fact that 98 per cent of the crude in that province was being exported, the right to deal with it and in effect to fix pricing was with the provincial government. That transaction was entirely within that province. This is the law as it now stands.
What would be the situation if British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan acquired Crown corporations with the jurisdiction to buy crude petroleum being produced at the wellhead? What is the position of such a corporation if it purchases from the producer the oil which is produced? Is it subject to this legislation? I see the minister is likely to answer yes. If that is the case, it is a good thing to know. In that case the province of Saskatchewan, which would be acquiring at the wellhead through the agency of a Crown corporation the crude petroleum being produced, would have to pay the price prescribed in this legislation.
What would be the situation if a provincial agency, corporation or individual in the private sector purchased the crude at the wellhead and sold it to an interprovincial pipeline in a transaction entirely within the province? What would be the situation if a corporation producing crude petroleum sold to a storage facility which is storing within the limits of the province? What would be the situation if a refinery acquired crude petroleum from producing wells and from people who own the producing wells within the province?
If a refinery purchases the crude, refines it, and then sells the petroleum partly in the province and partly outside it, does such a refinery have to buy at the price prescribed in this bill? This question goes to the heart of the situation. I have been talking about petroleum but the same applies to natural gas.
If one reads clause 36, clauses 40 to 44 inclusive, and the corresponding clauses dealing with natural gas, one can only reach the conclusion that transactions taking place entirely within a province are subject to the provisions of the legislation, and that people buying or selling must do so at the price prescribed unless a party to the transaction fulfils the onus of establishing, by documentary evidence to the satisfaction of the minister or his officials, that the transaction was limited to production purchased and sold entirely within a province. This would include provincial Crown agencies. This being the case there is no question that the provisions of the bill are repugnant to our present law and repugnant to the constitution, and for these reasons we feel they should not be supported except subject to the amendments we have put forward.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a couple of other remarks I would like to make. The hon. member for Peace River made mention of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan which have set up Crown corporations. Here again we in this party would certainly like to hear from the minister and get any kind of verbal commitments-although we are a little leery of that because we tried that before, over a year ago, and look what it got us. But supposing the minister were successful in negotiating a small, modest price increase with the Province of Saskatchewan, say 50 cents, or a dollar a barrel, and all of that extra money was to be spent by the Province of Saskatche-
29SS7-31

April 15, 1975
Oil and Petroleum
wan, through its Crown corporation-SaskOil-in exploration, research, development and production, would the minister then forget about counting that money against equalization? Will he assure us that the Minister of Justice will forget about taxing the Crown corporation?
If a producing province decides to take charge of the development of its energy resources, no matter what province, or whether it is oil, or gas, or some other form of energy, if there is a lack of leadership by the federal government and a lack of the provision of co-ordination, will the minister make it as easy as possible for them to do it? Or will he do otherwise in an effort to shore up-as I heard him say on television when he was being interviewed by the press a few Sundays ago-his own view that it goes against his grain personally if you are not using the private enterprise sector? I heard the minister say words to that effect on television on a national program.
Does that mean that, if any province wishes to launch into taking charge of the development of its energy resources, the minister will throw up any roadblocks he can to prevent SaskOil, or any other province? Does it mean that those provinces can look forward to all the roadblocks possible to prevent public ownership, operation and control of the development of their own energy resources? Unless we can get some indications about that from the minister he should be happy that we supported his bill in principle, let alone any way else. But what more can he tell us about his plans and his programs for the future?
Another point which was made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was also made by the premier of Saskatchewan. I am not going to be shy about repeating it. Again, if you are going to increase the present price and the consumers of Canada pay more for old oil so that you can find new oil, are the people of Canada going to pay more for that again? In other words, are the people to be expected to pay twice for security of supply of an energy source?
This brings me back to the logical and indisputable position taken by our party, and taken by the premier of Saskatchewan, that the only possible justification for any further increase in the price of old oil-the present national production-would be if the money were to be used only for exploration and development of oil and gas or other energy resources. In fact the premier of Saskatchewan in his submission did not just talk about oil and gas. He mentioned hydro electric power, which should make people in Nova Scotia happy when they keep proposing the Fundy project, or Manitoba or other provinces which really want to get into hydro electric development and other sources for developing electric energy, a lot of which will have to take the place of heating fuels in the years ahead. Extra money could be used now for other energy sources besides oil and gas.
The record of performance of the private sector has been good in its terms, but it has not been good in the long term for our country. I do not say the private sector was deliberately trying to hurt our country, not one bit. I do not blame them. Their objective was to make a profit, and this they did. They did very well at it. I might complain about it, but I do not blame them for it. That was their purpose.

They were there to make all the bucks they could-the multinationals-and they did very well at it. But the suggestion now, from here on in, that we have to rely on them to save us, is just nonsense. We just do not need them any more. We can do it ourselves.
I suppose it would be way too much to expect that hon. members across the way would agree to doing this in the most sensible way-that it all be done through public ownership, public enterprise. I guess that would be too much to expect. But even a mix of private and public Canadian enterprise is something we could do. There is no reason in the world why we could not. We can send Imperial Oil back to their bosses at Exxon, and we can send Gulf and Texaco and the rest of them home. There would be no problem. They have done well already. I do not see why they should need to do any better.
When the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain talked earlier about Alberta and Saskatchewan being able to steal, saying they can't reach an agreement but they can steal, I do not want to misquote him, but that is the way I understood him, I ask, who's been stealing from us? The very companies that have progressively reduced their research and exploration in both Alberta and Saskatchewan have continued to take larger and larger profits out of those two places.
Imperial Oil got $105 million in 1970, and then went up to $136 million in 1971-that is a 29 per cent increase. That is even better than the average runway sweeper got. In 1972 they went to $157 million, which was only a 15 per cent increase over 1971. In 1973 they rose to $228 million, a 45 per cent increase. That is when the exploration activities, whether by way of feet drilled or dollars spent, started to diminish. Their take home pay, if I may use a colloquial expression, went up by 45 per cent. Then in 1974 they jumped from $228 million to $290 million, a 27 per cent increase, yet what they spent on exploration went down even further.
They are now asking us for more money to explore and drill. If Canada wants its energy resources developed further, we need more dollars per barrel of oil, says Imperial Oil. I say no to Imperial Oil. In view of the record of what they have done, or perhaps what they have failed to do, in the last two years they have lost any right to expect or to ask for a further increase in the price of oil for their own benefit. This is especially so when they can give no assurance that they will spend any such increase on research and exploration in Canada, let alone in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
If the minister does not want to use Petro-Can or SaskOil, or some other Crown corporation, but insists on letting the multinationals have a piece of the action, why does he not put more teeth in his legislation and give the oil companies two choices in regard to exploration and development-that this is either compulsory or that they have to do it? If he would put that provision in the legislation he would get even stronger support for the bill from our party.
I do not question the minister's concern. He is responsible for the whole area of energy supply in Canada and I know he is making a conscientious effort to bring in
April 15, 1975

legislation and policies to try to alleviate this concern and provide more protection for the country in years ahead. But we are of the view that the minister is only going part of the way, that these half measures will not in fact accomplish the results that he and all of us want. They will not accomplish those results unless he opts to strengthen the legislation or opts for public development of future oil and gas reserves.
Saskatchewan would like to do this itself in regard to the oil fields that we know we have. This would eliminate an expensive form of development. We even have a small corner of the tar sands in Saskatchewan up in the Cold Lake area. But we have much more research and development to do in the handling of heavy crudes. We could refine our own heavy crude in Saskatchewan, but we are up to our eyeballs in asphalt, and what do we do with the asphalt? One kind westerner suggested that we should pave over Toronto and fill it full of wheat.
Saskatchewan would like to spend its oil profits on doing these things, but the Minister of Finance says that the deal is off for now. Two thirds of the money is put into the capital fund and will be counted against Saskatchewan for equalization purposes. This is going to cost Saskatchewan another $30 million to $40 million in equalization payments. We gave up $400 million by agreeing not to demand or try to get the world price, and I say $400 million is a fair contribution. Alberta has contributed three or four times that amount.
I also have the feeling that, even though the minister is a free enterpriser, his biggest problem is Alberta and the premier thereof. An agreement would have been much more readily reached had the federal government and the provinces been reasonably certain that there would not have been a lot of windfall money land in the tills of the big seven multinationals. The government knows that there is no way that the people of Canada will stand for that nonsense any more.
If my hon. friends of the Conservative party of Ontario could persuade their Conservative party friends of Alberta to do something more in a public way in regard to the future development of energy resources, and to make sure there would not be some more windfall rake-off, much of which would leave this country, then the chances of reaching an agreement between the federal government and the provinces would be much enhanced.
I suspect that the problems of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources are much less with Premier Bla-keney. It may well be that in his heart of hearts he would have liked to agree with the premier's proposal, lock, stock and barrel. He did say that there was a lot to be said for the proposal, that it was worthy of serious consideration, but that he could not buy the whole package. I suspect this is because of the free enterprise syndrome that still exists in the cabinet, and in some members of his party and of the Conservative party.
The one concrete proposal that made sure that the Canadian people would be given some assurance of energy supply, particularly of oil and gas, in decades ahead came from a producing province that is still looked upon as a have not province, and which has also led the way in forgoing revenue to which it was entitled. Even if I had a nightmare I would have a great deal of difficulty visualiz-
Oil and Petroleum
ing the province of Ontario willingly giving up as much as Alberta has Mr. Chairman. If the issue here were nickel, or iron ore, or steel, I can just see the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton rushing into this House of Commons and saying: "We want to forgo $1.5 billion a year on this development for the benefit of Canada". I would really like to see him do that. I did not hear anyone from this part of the country suggest, when the western provinces willingly went along with paying higher prices themselves, that they should pay an economic price.
This brings me to another point. We have two prices for oil and two prices for wheat. I find that very strange. I wish that someone from Ontario, Quebec or the Atlantic provinces would suggest two prices for forest products, or fertilizer, or farm machinery, or steel, or asbestos, or nickel. But, no, I hear no such suggestion. Why two prices just for oil and wheat?
My hon. friends to my right often talk of western alienation. They talk of it in different terms and for different reasons than I. They express the attitude of people who think it is their turn to get their hand in the till. They want to take the money and to hell with the rest of the country. We have put up with that sort of nonsense for too long as it is.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources might remind his colleague, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, about how much he would be able to lower the price of housing if there were a two price system for forest and lumber products. People pay hundreds of dollars per thousand feet of lumber to build a home. This has nothing to do with cost of production; this is the price of lumber on the international market. Builders and home buyers are forced to pay the international price, which is exorbitant and outrageous. But I hear no one talking about a two price system for forest products. I ask, why not?
I say that Saskatchewan has made its contribution. It has more than shown its willingness to co-operate and to reach agreement. Having reached agreement, the agreement was then thrown out the window. In carrying on his bilateral discussions I ask the minister to reassure the people of Saskatchewan in particular-and I wish the minister lots of luck when dealing with the government of Alberta-that anything agreed to from here on in will be lived up to. Forget all this nonsense about taxing not only oil companies' profits but oil companies' expenses; even I as a socialist find that difficult to live with. I am not known to have a great deal of love for multinational oil companies, but no matter what kind they are and how they operate you should still treat them fairly.
To continue to perpetuate or support the legislation which taxes not only their profits but their expenses, namely, the royalties they pay to the provinces, has to be an example of bad faith. If the minister would like more readiness to agree on the part of the provinces he should persuade the Minister of Finance to get rid of the prohibition on deductibility of royalties as an expense. That must go along with any increase in oil prices. That is a must. One must assume that the deductibility of royalties from the expenses of the oil companies for tax purposes will be allowed if that money is to be available for exploration

Oil and Petroleum
and development in respect of oil, gas, and other energy resources in this country.
Let me close by repeating a statement by the Premier of Saskatchewan at the first ministers' conference. I know the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources heard it, but I wish to refresh his memory. It is time for Canada and the provinces on behalf of their people to take charge of the development and exploration in respect of energy resources, oil, gas, hydro-electricity and so on.
We can no longer depend on others. If ever we could depend on them we certainly cannot now. We can no longer continue our supine acquiescence to the board rooms of the multinational corporations in Houston, Chicago or New York. When will we stand on our own feet? We have the people, the money, the technology and the resources. Why do we not do it? We can. It will take some will and imagination. It will excite the imagination of the Canadian people. It will be for the benefit of all the people in the country, and there will not be any fast-buck artists running around with 19th century ideologies making all the fast bucks they can, and then running. We can put an end to that.
The minister has a golden opportunity to make these moves. He, in concert with three or four provinces, whether they are of the same or opposite political stripe, can get together now and really have wells drilled around this country to an extent that would make it look like a Swiss cheese. We could be engaged in development that would make 1947 look like a bare beginning. We have the opportunity, and it is up to the minister and the government to seize that opportunity.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it must be obvious to the House that the time has come when we must face reality in respect of this bill. The position of Her Majesty's Official Opposition has been made abundantly clear, namely, that we believe the government needs some form of a bill in order to carry out the agreement of March 27, 1974, in connection with achieving one price across Canada.
We believe this bill is necessary to provide compensation for those parts of Canada which must buy their oil offshore. However, on the bringing in of such legislation we have put forward, over and over again, the proposition that it should be a bill that will stand the test of the constitution and of the courts of this land. This bill will not stand the test of the courts of this land. The evidence to this effect is preponderant. Therefore we will be proposing a dozen amendments in an effort to improve this bill and to save it from the courts if it should be challenged.
The second point I wish to make is that no bill passed by this parliament in the interests of democracy, as we understand it, should give perpetual power to a government to the extent this bill gives power to the government. So our amendments will be moved in an effort to give assurance to the people that, even though we want to give the government the power to carry out the decisions of this parliament in relation to doing these things to which all parties agree, we do not want to destroy the type of constitution and rule of law we have.
I said yesterday that no consensus will be arrived at under the early clauses of this bill on the question of the

price of oil, natural gas, or synthetic oil until the irrational and asinine budget of May and November is departed from. The retreat of Napoleon Bonaparte from Moscow will be nothing compared to the retreat the Minister of Finance will have to make on this silly budget of 1974. I notice that the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre has left the House. I know he is a serious student of Hansard and will read my remarks tomorrow.
In my remarks yesterday I put into layman's language the legal decisions dealing with the question of who owns these resources. I put into layman's language the decision of the courts of this land on the question of who can do what to whom with regard to taxes. All the jurisprudence says that under the constitution these resources belong to the provinces, and that the only level of government that has the right to tax these resources 100 per cent and take it all legally are the provincial governments of this country. Therefore, to translate this into layman's language, I said that the only governments that have the legal right to steal everything, whether they be civil rights, property rights or resource rights, are the provincial governments. I do not think any person can quarrel with this. That is the reason I referred to this as a silly budget that was passed in this House last November. It was an attempt to get the federal government in the same field where it would have the right to steal some of the resources belonging to the provinces.
We know that the Minister of Finance will have to retreat in respect of his budget and make some sort of arrangement with the provinces, and say that they will have the power to make these various royalties and taxes deductible up to a certain amount because, with everybody stealing so much, there will not be enough to keep things going.
I was amused by the remarks of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre because he must have known that some of us remember the oil play we had in Saskatchewan around 1950. The premier of the province at that time wrote to all the oil companies asking them to come to Saskatchewan. He said that so long as he was premier they would not be taken over.
You never saw such a free enterpriser as the premier of Saskatchewan in 1950. Now he can sit here and smile as one of the newcomers in the House speaks about what a great socialist he is. All I can say to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre is that he should make that speech to the steel workers of Hamilton. I will not deal with past records, although we know the provincial government of Alberta, ever since 1946, and the provincial government of Saskatchewan, the provincial government of Manitoba and the provincial government of British Columbia tried Canadian enterprise and turned over their resources of oil and gas completely to the international oil companies. They did that with amended types of regulations which they borrowed completely, word for word, from United States regulations.
The history of the betrayal by provincial governments of the people of those provinces is not what we are discussing here tonight. What we are discussing is what kind of government we are going to have in this country; will it
April 15, 1975

be one that is a strong central government and yet allows the provinces a certain place in the spectrum? This is the position of Her Majesty's Official Opposition and, I suggest, should be the position of every party in the House. The federal system we have is a unique central system of government. The federal system will not work if the central government, in the name of being efficient or strong, imposes on the rights and property of the provinces, and by provinces I mean the people of the provinces.
We have made our case as well as we know how. What we have to do now is to take this legislation step by step and do our level best to convince the government of the correctness of our approach. We cannot convince the NDP because they honestly and sincerely believe that the provinces should have no power and that they should become like municipalities. They want all the power at the centre. That is their philosophy, and they have a right to it. The Parti Quebecois has the right to call for separatism, as much as they have to call for all power to be at the centre. It is very clear how the NDP will stand, but it must be equally clear how we stand on our side of the House, and every person in the House must answer to the people of Canada.
I should like to remind the minister that there was a man who sat on his side of the House during the war and who received from the parliament in the crisis of those days the War Measures Act, and the War Supplies Act, which gave him all the powers that he needed to fight the war of 1939-1945. After the war was over, the War Measures Act was revoked.

The same thing will happen to this government. Canadians are very sensitive to an attempt by a government to take too much power into its hands. We are willing to give this power to the government in the case of an emergency and for a certain length of time, but every so often this legislation should be brought back to the House to see whether we will need it, because the day will come when the oil will be pouring out of the wells off the coast of Nova Scotia and off the coast of Labrador.

This bill should not become an act which forever hangs like a weight around the necks of Canadians.

Our amendments to the bill, which we will put forward tomorrow and as the debate rolls on, will all be aimed at trying to keep this bill within the walls of the constitutional framework that has protected and guided this country for over 100 years. We will try to persuade the government to look hard at some of these proposals which deal with some of the evils of the legislation which have not yet been mentioned in this debate, and which could more properly be dealt with when consideration is given to the clauses of the bill as they come up for debate.
I should like to suggest that we have said all we can say many times over, and it is up to the government now to make the decisions that have to be made, whether or not we produce a good bill. I think that is the issue before us tonight.
