subtopic: HEALTH-POSSIBILITY OF PROVINCES SHARING COST OF CHRONIC CARE HOSPITALS
HEALTH-POSSIBILITY OF PROVINCES SHARING COST OF CHRONIC CARE HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 28 I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) if he was considering sharing the cost of programs with the provinces which are now left out and which the provinces carry on their own, and which are an integral part of the health care cost field. I have always felt that the minister was a very humane person with a very sympathetic understanding of the health care field. This has prompted me to urge him further to enter those fields of health care in which the federal government is not now participating.
The provinces are finding it increasingly difficult to meet those costs, and whether one is actively sick or chronically ill, care is still necessary. In the last meeting with the provinces the minister agreed to discuss and accept participation in lower cost areas if restraint could be practised in higher cost areas. I hope that this will be arranged.
It is true that active treatment costs might be cut by sending a patient to convalescent care a day or two sooner, or by sending him to his home and providing someone to give the necessary care. How do you remedy this situation and arrange for that further care outside active treatment for these patients? Let us be quite honest about this at the start when there is talk about active treatment beds and increasing costs.
[The Chairman.]
Indeed, if the active treatment beds were not occupied, it would mean there would be no doctor or nursing case required. But the cost would go down by only 20 per cent on hospital care. It follows then that it is a losing proposition to the taxpayer to have a hospital bed empty because the hospital staff and administration and upkeep costs continue. Thus the maximum use will likely be made of every bed in an active treatment hospital.
When a patient is ready to be transferred to chronic care or convalescent care, there is often no bed to which the patient can go. If the patient is sent home, there is often no one or no system to provide the proper care or attention required. Probably only a minimal amount of nursing care is required, but it is required around the clock. This should be a shared cost.
While home care at present does help, it does not meet the necessary requirements in the patient's own home. An eight hour shift does not meet the patient's needs for 24 hours. Yet it would be much cheaper to provide that care than to keep the patient in an active treatment bed in hospital.
When the patient is ready to go to a chronic care nursing home where the bed costs are approximately half that of an active treatment bed, we find that he or she has to spend weeks waiting for a bed in a chronic care nursing home. Over and over again I have heard that there are many chronic care beds in my constituency, but I have found that for periods of ten days or longer a patient often cannot get into one of these institutions.
In a chronic care nursing home the cost is $18.50 per day-this was increased from $17 on April 1, 1975-which leaves the patient paying $5.90 per day unless he is under the age of 16 years. This is a saving, on the average, of approximately $60 plus per day when compared with an active treatment bed, or $20 per day in a chronic care bed in hospital.
Nursing homes have the same economic pressures and labour costs as do hospitals, yet the government allows nursing care from one and a half to two and a half hours, and the patient load is eight to ten per attendant. For a patient who is chronically ill, this is probably more than an attendant can look after properly.
It would seem to me that we need to fund nursing homes or give incentives to allow them to make more beds available. This would relieve the situation and cut the costs of chronic care units by at least 50 per cent, and of transfer from an active treatment bed to a chronic care bed from around $80 to $18.50 per day. Obviously the place where the federal government can share cost to the greatest advantage and get the best value for its tax dollar is the nursing home.
I bring this to the attention of the minister in the hope that rising health costs will be met by efficiency in treatment and, with an aging population which is so often found in the nursing home, to carry it further by stating that all residential homes should carry 5 per cent of their beds as chronic care beds so that old people may be treated there for minor illnesses. This would not only be a financial saving but would be humane for the older person.
To summarize, Mr. Speaker, nursing care homes should be a shared health care cost. Home care costs, where
April 15, 1975

feasible, should be a shared health care cost around the clock where necessary until the patient has a reasonable recovery time. All homes for the elderly should have sick bay units where those not needing full time hospitalization, or having minor illnesses, could be treated at the home as a shared health cost thus avoiding the trauma and expense of moving, and the expense of an active treatment bed.
The health resources program should establish a chair of geriatric medicine in all medical schools. This should be a demand program to meet the needs of the rapidly increasing elderly population with diseases peculiar to their age group. We have today only 26 or 27 geriatricians in the whole of Canada. This is a grossly neglected area when you think that at the other end of the scale there are around 1,000 pediatricians.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-POSSIBILITY OF PROVINCES SHARING COST OF CHRONIC CARE HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal government is well aware of the matter raised by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard). In fact discussions began on this matter four years ago at the health ministers' conference held in November, 1970, at which time support was expressed for a re-examination of existing arrangements for health financing with the aim of developing an alternative to them. The stated objective was to encourage a rational, efficient and flexible reorganization of the health delivery system to increase effectiveness and reduce waste of costly resources.
Following nearly two and a half years of discussions and negotiation, the formal federal offer on health financing was placed before provincial governments at the federal-provincial conference of finance and health ministers in May, 1973, and was considered further at the first ministers' conference on May 25, 1973. The offer included a formula for grant payments related to GNP growth and a $640 million trust fund; it was designed to provide a reasonable rate of growth in the basic federal payments, a degree of risk-sharing, flexibility for the provinces to determine their own priorities, and assistance in the development of more effective and efficient systems of health delivery.
An important condition attached to the offer was that existing national standards of comprehensiveness, accessibility, universality and portability were to be retained with respect to the basic hospital and medical services. The federal offer also made it clear that the sharing of costs of major new health programs, such as denticare or pharmacare, would be a subject of separate discussion, if and when a consensus was developed by the provinces.
Following this conference, the provincial premiers met in August, 1973, and requested their ministers of health to develop a common provincial response to the federal proposal. It was more than a year later, at a meeting last September 25, that they produced a resolution which rejected the federal offer and outlined their position on new health financing arrangements. Of considerable significance in this resolution was the statement by the provinces that they were prepared to negotiate changes in cost-sharing of high-cost services in exchange for federal sharing in programs not now supported.
Adjournment Debate
At the conference of ministers of health in January of this year the minister advised the provincial ministers that the federal offer of a per capita grant had now been withdrawn. There followed a discussion of various proposals, including a specific proposal put forward by the government of Quebec. In the light of the discussion the minister then suggested a new approach based on the expressed willingness of the provinces to restrain the growth of high cost services in return for federal sharing in other areas not now supported. This proposal involves a broader interpretation of existing legislation which could permit additional cost-sharing.
The ministers agreed with the proposed approach and directed their deputy ministers to undertake immediately negotiations aimed at improving cost effectiveness and comprehensiveness of health care delivery systems, within the context of present legislative authority. The objective will be improvement in health care planning and development through a more flexible approach to financing, with continued emphasis on provincial priorities. The negotiations will entail identification of measures to restrain the growth of high cost services that provinces would be prepared to adopt in order to permit extension of federal sharing to equally effective but lower cost alternatives. Deputy ministers were asked to submit their recommendations no later than September 15 of this year.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PERMITTING ENTRY OF VALENTYN MOROZ AND FAMILY AS LANDED IMMIGRANTS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PERMITTING ENTRY OF VALENTYN MOROZ AND FAMILY AS LANDED IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 13 I attempted to move the following motion:
That the Prime Minister and the government of Canada convey to the government of the USSR the feeling of the people of Canada that they are willing to permit entry into Canada of Valentyn Moroz and his family as landed immigrants.
I did not get the unanimous consent that is required to debate the motion. During the question period I therefore asked the minister whether he would give consideration to this proposal. The minister replied that he would examine the question and give it consideration.
I then asked the minister if he would arrange for representatives of the Canadian government in the Soviet Union to ascertain the state of health of Valentyn Moroz. I did this because of information which has come to light that Moroz, while in prison, has been beaten and stabbed, that he is now in poor health and in the middle of a hunger strike. The minister suggested he would not do as I asked. He said, as recorded on page 3181 of Hansard for February 13, 1975:
... I have not agreed to such a move as in the circumstances I think it would very likely be counterproductive.
Valentyn Moroz was born in the Ukraine, which is part of the Soviet Socialist Republic. He attended the University of Lviv, where he majored in history. After graduation he taught history and geography. In 1965, he was arrested, charged with anti-Soviet propaganda and agitation, and sentenced to four years of hard labour.

April 15, 1975
Adjournment Debate
In 1970, he was again arrested, tried, and sentenced to a long prison term. While in prison he has been beaten, stabbed, and, as I say, he is now in the midst of a hunger strike.
In November, 1972, Amnesty International, known for its non-partisan, non-political work on behalf of prisoners in every country who are being persecuted by a government, reported that Moroz had been gravely wounded by some criminal inmates in the prison in which he was incarcerated. After that he was transported to a prison hospital in Kiev.
In May, 1974, many of our most prominent Canadian authors and academics made an appeal on behalf of Valen-tyn Moroz in the Soviet Union. Among their numbers are included Pierre Berton, June Callwood, Professor Crowe of York University, Professor Eayrs of the University of Toronto, Northrop Frye, of that same university, Professor Gerald LeDain, who headed the commission study on drugs on behalf of the Government of Canada, Peyton Lyon, a professor at Carleton University, and many others. They all addressed an open appeal to the authorities of the Soviet Union.
As I say, since his imprisonment Moroz has been beaten, stabbed and confined with the criminally insane. Reports since January, 1974, indicate that he is confined to an isolation cell, where he is being pressured to recant. He is in extremely poor physical and mental condition, and concerned circles in the Soviet Union have expressed fears that he may not survive present treatment. The recently expelled dissident, Pavel Litvinov, has stated that Moroz will begin a hunger strike until death on the fourth anniversary of his arrest if his conditions are not changed.
People have appealed to the Soviet authorities to permit Moroz to leave prison. The minister said, when replying to my question, that my proposal would be counterproductive. That opinion might have been valid during the years whfen Stalin ruled Soviet Russia. But the Soviets have changed. They react to international public opinion. Solzhenitsyn was expelled, not imprisoned. Rostropovich was relieved of his passport after he left Russia, as was Medved. Pavel Litvinov, grandson of Maxim Litvinov, was permitted to leave. Thousands of Soviet Jews have been permitted to leave. Most have gone to Israel, but many are in Canada.
I make two proposals. First, I suggest that the government should tell the Soviet authorities that if Moroz's views are such that he cannot be permitted to live in freedom in that country, this country would welcome him and his family. Canada has already become known to hundreds of thousands of Ukranians. Second, the government should ask Soviet authorities to permit representatives of this country to visit Moroz in prison so that those who are concerned about his well-being, his health, can be assured that his health has not been broken, as he and his family allege, but that, indeed, he is well physically, mentally and emotionally, as Soviet authorities claim. I urge the government to act along the lines I suggested.

speakeroldname: Mr. Herb Breau (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PERMITTING ENTRY OF VALENTYN MOROZ AND FAMILY AS LANDED IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians have actively taken up the cause of Mr. Moroz with a view to improving his living conditions in prison and ensuring
[Mr. Orlikow.|
that his state of health is good. They have also called for his release from prison and have supported the idea of his emigration from the Soviet Union, possibly even to Canada, although we have no evidence that Mr. Moroz himself desires this.
The government has taken a keen interest in questions relating to human rights wherever they arise. That said, however, the government is faced with a number of considerations that must be taken into account in deciding what role it might be able to play. As the representative of the people of Canada, it is turned to by Canadians to make representations for them to the Soviet authorities on Mr. Moroz's behalf. On the other hand, its possibilities for action on behalf of the nationals of other countries are limited by international considerations. The Canadian government respects the right of other governments to run the internal affairs of their countries, just as it expects other governments to respect its right to do so. This is a fundamental principle of international law and diplomatic relations among nations.
It is, of course, possible for the Canadian government to express the concern of its citizens over violations of human rights, and it has done so frequently. However, if Canada is to have any influence on the course of events in the Soviet Union, or anywhere else, we have to take a hard look at the effect that acting on the various possibilities open to us would have. If our voice is to be listened to on such matters, it will be only if the Soviet government respects our intentions and motives.
A slamming of the door is what would happen if the Government of Canada went beyond the bounds of what is regarded as acceptable in dealings between nations. When I see that, as a result of the quality of the relations that we and others have developed with the USSR, several thousand more Jews have emigrated from there to Israel, and several hundred more Soviet citizens have been able to join their families in Canada and elsewhere, I am anxious that there should be no slamming of doors.
To return to the specific question of Mr. Moroz, the Canadian government and Canadian officials have raised this case with the Soviet authorities a number of times in light of the humanitarian considerations involved and as a reflection of the concern of Canadians. As far back as 1971 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took the opportunity of Soviet Premier Kosygin's visit to Ottawa to speak to him about this case. In September the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) spoke to Foreign Minister Gromyko in New York in view of the reports of Mr. Moroz's deteriorating health. He assured him then that Mr. Moroz's health was satisfactory in all respects. Later reports that came to our attention on this subject were disquieting and further inquiries were made of the Soviet Ambassador in November. The ambassador assured us that the information received from Mr. Gromyko remained valid.
There have been suggestions that the government should seek his release from prison, or otherwise take a position on the merits of his case. Quite apart from the impropriety of making such approaches to the Soviet government on behalf of a non-Canadian, we believe that adopting such a course would require information on the case to which the Canadian government does not have
April 15, 1975

access, nor any claim to access. We simply do not have a right to call for information on which to base a judgment of the merits of such cases.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-DISCUSSIONS WITH UNITED STATES CONCERNING TRANSPORTATION OF ALASKAN OIL ACROSS CANADA
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-DISCUSSIONS WITH UNITED STATES CONCERNING TRANSPORTATION OF ALASKAN OIL ACROSS CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as some hon. members know, as long ago as 1971 the government of the day under the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a definite decision to discourage any oil pipeline from Alaska southerly along the Mackenzie valley and then southerly across Canada to the United States. This, of course, caused a great deal of debate, especially with regard to the fears raised by those in British Columbia who understandably were and still are concerned with the problems posed by tankers bringing Alaskan oil down the west coast of British Columbia through the narrow Straits of Juan de Fuca to refineries in the State of Washington. That concern, as I said, still exists.
In October of 1974, the then U.S. ambassador-at-large, William Eberle, was in Canada for several days. He made comments which clearly indicated that the United States was looking to the development of sources of oil for petroleum in the State of Alaska other than in the Prudhoe Bay area.
In the remarks the minister made it became obvious that it might very well be United States policy to ship that Alaskan oil out by means of a cross-Canada oil line down the Mackenzie to the continental United States. On October 10, 1974, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) whether he knew that discussions had taken place between United States officials and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) concerning this particular proposal.
I also asked whether it was Canada's intention to use the desire of the United States to establish an oil pipe line across Canada as a lever in negotiations to persuade the Americans to take the tankers out of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. The Secretary of State was non-commital in his answer, but he did not deny that such discussions had taken place, and recently there has been increasing speculation that American policy is looking to a trans-Canada pipe line route.
Today, my colleague, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), was able to put a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on this very point. The minister answered by saying that no specific proposal had been put forward by the United States in respect to an oil pipe line but that extensive discussions had taken place
Adjournment Debate
between Canadian and United States officials with respect to a pipe line treaty which would govern the construction of any pipe line, either in Canada or the United States.
My question is specific, and in all the circumstances it requires a clear answer. Have any discussions gone on, or are any discussions going on, between Canada and the United States relating to an oil pipe line from Alaska through the Mackenzie Valley, and south from Canada to the United States? If not, have the Americans asked for any such discussions to take place, and what has been the Canadian response? Further, I would ask whether it is within the knowledge of the Canadian government that it is United States policy to negotiate with Canada with respect to arrangements which would enable Alaskan oil to be carried by oil pipe line across Canada to the United States?

speakeroldname: Mr. Herb Breau (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-DISCUSSIONS WITH UNITED STATES CONCERNING TRANSPORTATION OF ALASKAN OIL ACROSS CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government position of strong opposition to the movement of oil in large tankers into the Puget Sound area has long been made clear. This position was made known to the United States administration at an early stage, and the Canadian government proposed that Canada and the United States explore together the possibility of alternate supply routes for the Pacific Northwest area of the United States. The United States agreed, and this course of action has been actively pursued, notably at meetings in Ottawa and Washington in August, 1974 and February, 1975.
In addition we are discussing with the United States such matters as vessel traffic management, environmental control, contingency planning and liability arrangements with a view to minimizing the possibility of oil spills and providing for clean-ups should they occur. These arrangements will have considerable value in themselves whether or not increased tanker traffic develops in these waters.
In the short term, a pipe line through Canada to carry Alaskan oil to market would not be feasible as an alternative to the Alyeska line.
In the longer term it is conceivable that sufficient oil might be available in the Arctic to justify a second pipe line which could transport both Canadian and Alaskan arctic oil. However, the necessary reserves have not been discovered. In addition, a number of factors would be involved in a decision to build such a pipe line. Having regard to the complexity of this question it would be premature to make any concrete assessment of this possibility at the present stage.
The hon. member asked me two specific questions this evening, one of which I do not think I have dealt with, but I will check into it and see that he gets the information.
